chains.d: How the form of an argument came to be separated from what the argument is about: Aristotle's schematic letters and the first proof that some forms reduce to others; the Stoic forms that work on whole propositions rather than terms; Frege's quantifiers, which finally allowed one sentence to carry two generalities; and the Tractatus attempt to make the whole of logic fall out of a truth-table. The entries run in the order in which expressive power was won, and each names what its predecessor could not say.

chains.n: Contradiction, and the refusals of it
chains.d: Four positions on what a contradiction is and what may be done with one: the Eleatic ban on not-being that makes change unsayable; Aristotle's argument that non-contradiction cannot be demonstrated and must instead be defended by refuting the denier; the four-cornered negation of Madhyamaka, which declines all four positions rather than choosing among them; and Hegel's dialectic, which is placed here to mark where formalisation stops. The order is the order of the site's timeline; it is not a record of who read whom.

Five arguments that try to get an existence claim out of the analysis of a concept, and the objections that made the attempt famous. The order is the order of the quarrel: Anselm's reductio, Gaunilo's parody of its schema, Descartes' perfection-based restatement, Kant's charge that existence is not a predicate at all, and the twentieth-century modal repair that concedes Kant's point and relocates the burden.

Five arguments that begin from some feature of the world -- contingency, a beginning, causal dependence, order -- and reason back to a first term. They are set in the order in which each one sharpened the last: Avicenna's necessary existent, al-Ghazali's argument from a beginning, Aquinas's per se causal regress, Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason, and Hume's dismantling of the design version, which reaches back over the whole chain.

Whether the power, knowledge and goodness ascribed to God can be squared with the suffering that is actually observed. The entries sit in this order because each accepts the previous one's terms and then changes them: a statement of the inconsistency, two attempts to dissolve it, and finally the argument that consistency was never the difficulty.

Whether anything is open, given that what will happen is already true, already fated, or already known. The order tracks a single argument that survives each diagnosis by reappearing in a stronger form: from truth-value, to fate, to timeless knowledge, to the fixity of the past.

Whether any belief can be shown to be warranted, and what happens to the demand for warrant when it is pressed without stopping. The entries sit in this order because each answers the one before it: the ancient statement of the problem, the foundationalist attempt to halt it, Hume's demonstration that the same problem defeats the empiricist alternative, the twentieth-century attempt to do without justification and keep only refutation, and the holist reply that refutation lands on a conjunction and so settles nothing by itself.

What a formal treatment of language is forced to distinguish, and what it turns out not to be able to define. The order is one of inheritance: Russell answers Frege's puzzle without admitting senses, the positivists build a criterion of meaningfulness on Russell's method of analysis, and Quine turns the demand for a non-circular criterion back on the notion of meaning that the whole programme had been resting on.

chains.n: Universals, identity and what there is
chains.d: Whether a predicate shared by many things answers to a single entity they share. The chain runs from the principle Plato needs, through the regress that principle generates, to the nominalist's demand for economy, to the moment the principle was finally written down as an axiom and proved contradictory, and ends with the account of identity that survived the wreck.

Whether a conclusion about what ought to be can rest on premises about what is. Hume states the gap as a claim about vocabulary, Kant relocates the ought in the form of a maxim rather than in any fact, Mill attempts the crossing directly, and Moore argues that no crossing is available at all.

Whether anything beyond one's own mind can be known, and whether the question is even well posed. The entries sit in this order because each takes over the previous one's materials: Descartes manufactures the doubt with a principle about knowledge, Berkeley tries to dissolve it by denying that there is an outside, and Moore keeps every proposition of the sceptical argument and reverses the direction of inference.

What authority over persons and holdings can be justified, and by what kind of argument. Hobbes reasons from a strategic predicament to the necessity of a sovereign; Rawls asks which principles would be chosen under enforced ignorance; Nozick argues that any principle specifying a distribution must be bought at the price of continual interference. Each is a decision-theoretic argument, and each turns on a step that decision theory cannot settle.

args.sub: that a first-figure syllogism holds by its form alone, and that the other figures can be proved to reduce to it
args.work: Prior Analytics I.1-7, c. 350 BCE
args.sysn: Aristotle's assertoric syllogistic, set beside the modern first-order rendering
args.claim: That from 'A belongs to every B' and 'B belongs to every C' it follows of necessity that A belongs to every C, in virtue of the arrangement of the terms and nothing else; and that every other valid mood can be reduced by proof to this one and to Celarent.
key: Aristotle's schematic letters, standing for general terms, not for individuals; their introduction is usually counted the first use of variables in logic
A belongs to every B, the universal affirmative; the medieval vowel notation, not Aristotle's
A belongs to no B, the universal negative
A belongs to some B, the particular affirmative
the same terms read as one-place predicates in the modern rendering
x is a head of y

lines.d: Aristotle's gloss on 'belongs to every' at 24b28-30: nothing can be taken under the subject term of which the predicate term is not said.
lines.note: The gloss is stated in terms of what can be taken, not of a domain of objects. Reading it as a quantification over a domain is already a modern move.

lines.d: A belongs to every B. Every proposition in the system relates two general terms; there are no names, no singular subjects, and no relational predicates anywhere in it.
B belongs to every C. B is the middle term, and it is its position, predicate in one premise and subject in the other, that makes the figure first.
Prior Analytics I.4, 25b37-40. Aristotle states the mood as a conditional with a necessity inside the consequent, not as a licence to write a therefore.
lines.note: The necessity attaches to the consequence, not to the conclusion taken alone. Medieval logicians made the distinction explicit as necessitas consequentiae against necessitas consequentis; misreading it turns a valid form into a modal fallacy.

lines.d: A belongs to every C. Nothing has been assumed about what A, B and C mean, which is the whole point: the conclusion follows from the shape of the premises.

lines.f: {Eab ↔ Eba, Iab ↔ Iba, Aab → Iba} ⊢ every valid mood reduces to Barbara or Celarent
lines.d: By the conversion rules, by reduction per impossibile, and by ekthesis, Aristotle argues at I.7, 29b1 that the second and third figures can be completed through the two universal moods of the first.
lines.note: This is a claim about the system rather than within it, and it is the first metalogical result: a proof about which proofs are eliminable. What the notation shows is that a proof system can itself be an object of proof.

lines.d: The modern rendering. It is valid with no assumption that any term is non-empty, which matters because several moods Aristotle accepts are not.
lines.note: Darapti, from Aab and Acb to Iac, requires that B be non-empty; on the modern reading with possibly empty terms it fails. Aristotle's terms are always instantiated, so the divergence is a difference of presupposition, not an error.

lines.d: Every man is an animal, therefore every head of a man is a head of an animal. De Morgan's example from the logic of relations, 1864, and it is valid.
lines.note: Neither the premise nor the conclusion can be written in the syllogistic at all, because H is two-place and because the conclusion needs a universal and an existential in one sentence. This is the gap that stayed open for twenty-two centuries.

args.verdict: Valid, and valid in modern logic too: line 7 is a theorem of first-order logic requiring no existential import. The reduction claim at line 6 is also correct for the moods Aristotle accepts. The system's defect is not unsoundness but poverty: line 8 exhibits a valid inference the syllogistic cannot even state.
args.contested: What is disputed is not the validity of Barbara but the standing of the system. Łukasiewicz (1951) read the syllogistic as an axiomatic theory of term-relations with the moods as theorems; Corcoran (1974) and Smiley (1973) read it instead as a natural-deduction system in which the moods are derivations, which fits Aristotle's talk of completing imperfect syllogisms far better. Whether Aristotle's premises carry existential import by stipulation or by an assumption about scientific terms is likewise argued, and it decides whether Darapti is a mistake or a different convention.
args.why: The letters show that validity is a matter of arrangement: the same three schemata support the inference whatever terms replace them, and this is visible only once the terms are gone. Line 6 shows something further, that a system of proofs can be reasoned about from outside. And line 8 shows the exact boundary of the achievement by displaying a valid argument whose premise cannot be written in the notation, which is what makes Frege's later entry necessary rather than merely convenient.
args.anachronism: The vowel notation Aab, the mood-names Barbara and Celarent, and the very idea of a formal language are all medieval or later; Aristotle writes out 'A belongs to every B' in Greek and reasons about it in prose. The first-order rendering at line 7 imports a domain of objects and a treatment of the copula that the term logic does not have.

args.sub: that every valid argument can be reduced to five undemonstrated forms which operate on whole propositions
args.work: the logical works are lost; the system is reported by Sextus Empiricus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism II, and Diogenes Laertius VII.76-81. Chrysippus headed the Stoa c. 230 BCE
args.sysn: Stoic propositional logic, in which the variables are ordinal words standing for complete propositions
args.claim: That there are five argument forms which need no demonstration because their validity is evident, that every other valid argument can be reduced to them by a set of meta-rules, and that the variables of logic are whole propositions rather than terms.
key: propositional variables. The Stoics wrote 'the first' and 'the second': the schema of the opening form is reported as 'if the first, then the second; but the first; therefore the second'
the Stoic disjunction is exclusive and exhaustive: exactly one disjunct holds, which is why the fourth form below is valid for them and not for us
temporal operators, 'it was always the case that' and 'it will always be the case that', used to render Diodorus' criterion

lines.d: The first indemonstrable. If the first, then the second; but the first; therefore the second. The variables are ordinal words, and they stand for complete sayables, not for terms.
lines.note: This is the point of the whole system. Aristotle's letters go where a term goes; the Stoic ordinals go where a sentence goes, and that difference is the difference between term logic and propositional logic.

lines.d: The second. If the first, then the second; but not the second; therefore not the first.
The third, built on the negated conjunction rather than on the conditional. Not both the first and the second; but the first; therefore not the second.
The fourth. Either the first or the second; but the first; therefore not the second.
The fifth. Either the first or the second; but not the second; therefore the first.

lines.f: v(p) = T, v(q) = T: v(p ∨ q) = T, v(p) = T, v(¬q) = F
lines.d: A countermodel to the fourth form if disjunction is read inclusively, as modern logic reads it. Both disjuncts true makes the premises true and the conclusion false.
lines.note: The fourth form is therefore not classically valid, and its presence in the list is direct evidence that the Stoic disjunction is exclusive. The fifth survives either reading. The notation converts a question of translation into a question with an answer.

lines.f: if p, q ⊢ r then p, ¬r ⊢ ¬q
lines.d: The first thema, a meta-rule for reducing complex arguments to the indemonstrables. A third, a form of cut, is preserved in Alexander of Aphrodisias.
lines.note: The second and fourth themata are lost. Bobzien (1996) reconstructed them from Alexander and Simplicius and argued that the resulting system is deductively complete for the Stoic fragment; the reconstruction is not itself ancient testimony.

lines.d: The three competing truth conditions for the conditional. Callimachus reports that even the crows on the rooftops caw about which conditionals are true.
lines.note: Philo's is the material conditional exactly. Diodorus' is a temporal strengthening; Chrysippus' requires that the contradictory of the consequent be incompatible with the antecedent, which is a connexive or strict conditional and makes the conditional stronger than the modern one.

lines.f: (p → q) ≡ ¬(p ∧ ¬q) ⊢ the first and second forms
lines.d: On Philo's reading the five forms become, apart from the fourth, the classical rules of modus ponens, modus tollens, modus ponendo tollens and disjunctive syllogism.
lines.note: The conditional that modern logic uses is Philo's, not Chrysippus'. The logician who gave the system its shape lost the argument about its central connective.

args.verdict: Forms one, two, three and five are valid on any of the three readings of the conditional and on either reading of disjunction. The fourth is valid only if disjunction is exclusive, as line 6 shows. The claim that all valid arguments reduce to the five is a completeness claim that depends on the reconstructed themata and cannot be checked against a surviving text.
args.contested: Whether the Stoics had a genuine deductive system or a collection of schemata was long doubted; Mates (1953) and Frede (1974) established the first, and Bobzien's reconstruction of the themata pushed the claim further to completeness. The conditional debate is a real ancient controversy, reported by Sextus at Outlines II.110-112 and by Cicero, but the attribution of the third position to Chrysippus rests on Cicero and Diogenes rather than on Chrysippus' own words. Some scholars read his criterion as strict implication, others as genuinely connexive, and the two differ on whether a proposition may imply itself. Sextus in fact ranks four accounts in order of strength at that passage: Philo's, Diodorus', the connection or cohesion criterion, and a fourth on which the consequent is potentially contained in the antecedent. The three set beside each other here are the first three, and the attribution of the connection criterion to Chrysippus rests on Diogenes VII.73 rather than on Sextus, who names no one.
args.why: Putting the five side by side makes visible what no paraphrase does: they are closed under nothing but the arrangement of whole sentences, so the Stoic system is operating one level below Aristotle's, not competing with him on the same ground. Line 6 then converts a scholarly gloss about exclusive disjunction into a two-row countermodel. And line 8 sets three rival truth conditions in a single notation, which shows that the debate is not verbal and that the survivor is the weakest of the three.
args.anachronism: The Stoics had no truth-tables and no semantics of valuations; line 6 is a modern instrument applied to an ancient list. The turnstile and the arrow are anachronistic throughout, and rendering Diodorus with tense operators imports a modern temporal logic onto a criterion he stated in ordinary Greek about times.

args.sub: that the two readings of 'every boy loves some girl' differ in the order of two operators and in nothing else
args.work: Begriffsschrift, 1879
args.sysn: first-order logic with relational predicates and nested quantifiers
args.claim: That generality is expressed by an operator binding a variable, that such operators may be nested inside one another, and that sentences ambiguous in ordinary language are thereby resolved into distinct formulas with distinct truth conditions.
key: an arbitrary one-place predicate, used in stating Frege's definition of the existential quantifier

lines.d: One English sentence, with one syntactic parse and no lexical ambiguity: every word in it is used in a single sense.
The first reading. Each boy has some girl or other whom he loves, and different boys may love different girls.
lines.note: The existential lies inside the scope of the universal, so the value of y may depend on the value of x. That dependence is the entire content of the reading.

lines.d: The second reading. There is one particular girl whom every boy loves.
lines.note: The same two quantifiers, the same two predicates, the same relation. Only the order of binding differs, and nothing in the English marks the difference.

lines.d: The wide-scope reading entails the narrow-scope one. If there is a girl loved by every boy, then every boy loves some girl.
lines.note: This direction holds in every model, with no proviso needed; it is the interchange in the other direction that fails.

lines.d: A countermodel to the converse. Two boys, two girls, each boy loving one girl and a different one. Line 2 is true in this model and line 3 is false.
lines.note: Four individuals settle a question about the logical form of an English sentence. Nothing about the sentence's vocabulary could have settled it.

lines.d: Frege's own system has only the conditional stroke, the negation stroke, and the concavity with a Gothic letter for generality; the existential quantifier is defined, not primitive.
lines.note: The Begriffsschrift notation is two-dimensional and was read by almost no one. Peirce, with O. H. Mitchell, arrived at a quantifier notation independently in 1883-85, and it is Peirce's linear style, transmitted through Schröder and Peano, that modern logic actually writes.

lines.f: no term-logic form separates line 2 from line 3
lines.d: In the syllogistic both readings must be forced into a universal affirmative with a compound predicate, which collapses the distinction rather than expressing it.
lines.note: The reason is structural: Aristotle's syllogistic attaches at most one quantity to a proposition, at the subject; medieval supposition theory added scope devices the moods themselves never carry.

lines.d: The ambiguity is an ambiguity of scope. It lives in the order of two operators, and it is invisible in a language that has no operators to order.
lines.note: The same distinction is what makes uniform continuity different from continuity, and Cauchy's difficulties with the two are a case of the ambiguity doing damage before anyone had the notation to see it.

args.verdict: Not an argument with a contested premise but a demonstration, and it succeeds. The entailment at line 4 is valid; its converse is invalid, and the countermodel at line 5 is a complete proof of that. What is established is an expressive claim: first-order logic distinguishes two readings that term logic identifies.
args.contested: Not the logic, which is settled, but the linguistics and the history. Whether natural-language scope ambiguity is best treated by quantifier raising, by type-shifting, or by underspecification is an open question in semantics, and some linguists deny that the sentence has two readings rather than one general reading with pragmatic strengthening. On priority, Frege published first, in 1879, but Peirce and Mitchell developed quantification independently by 1885, and van Heijenoort's placing of Frege at the origin has been criticised by Putnam and others as understating the algebraic tradition.
args.why: Two formulas differing only in the order of two symbols have different truth conditions, and a model with four individuals proves it. The prose sentence gives no purchase at all: there is no word to point at, no equivocation to allege, nothing to disambiguate by rewording without already having made the distinction. This is the clearest case on the site of notation showing something the English hides completely, and it is also the reason the syllogistic could not have been repaired from inside.
args.anachronism: Frege wrote none of these formulas. His notation is a branching two-dimensional diagram in which the conditional is a horizontal-and-vertical stroke figure and generality is a concavity in the content stroke; the linear form here is Peano's and Russell's. The example sentence is a twentieth-century teaching device, not Frege's.

args.sub: that all propositions are truth-functions of elementary propositions, and that logic therefore says nothing
args.work: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 4.31, 5, 5.5, 6; written 1918, published 1921 and in English 1922
args.sysn: truth-functional propositional logic, with Wittgenstein's single operator of joint negation
args.claim: That every proposition is a truth-function of elementary propositions, that every truth-function results from repeated application of a single operation of joint negation, and that logical truths are consequently degenerate cases which say nothing about the world.
key: the truth value of P under a given assignment
a truth-function, that is, a mapping from assignments of truth values to a truth value
a class of propositions, written by Wittgenstein with a bar over a variable
joint negation: true if and only if every member of X is false
the general form of the proposition at Tractatus 6, given as the specification of a series
an arbitrary one-place predicate; a, b, c are individuals

lines.d: Tractatus 5: a proposition is a truth-function of elementary propositions, an elementary proposition being a truth-function of itself.
lines.note: The thesis is not that some propositions are truth-functional but that all are. Everything the entry turns on is in that quantifier.

lines.d: What being a truth-function amounts to. The truth-table of 4.31 is Wittgenstein's own device for displaying it, arrived at independently of Post and of Peirce's earlier unpublished tables.
lines.note: A truth-table is a definition, not a proof procedure, and it is finite. Both facts matter to what follows.

lines.d: The N-operator, joint negation. Applied to a single proposition it is negation; applied to a pair it is the connective now written NOR.
lines.note: Sheffer had shown in 1913 that one binary connective suffices. Wittgenstein's ambition is larger: one operation, applied to arbitrary classes, generating every proposition whatever. Peirce had reached the same result in an unpublished paper of 1880, which stayed unknown until the Collected Papers, so the priority here runs as it does for the truth-table itself.

lines.f: ¬p = N(p)   p ∨ q = N(N(p, q))   p ∧ q = N(N(p), N(q))
lines.d: The familiar connectives recovered from N alone. The reduction is correct and easily checked on the tables.
lines.note: This part of the thesis is simply true, and it is the part that gets remembered.

lines.d: The general form of the proposition, Tractatus 6: the first term is the class of elementary propositions, the second an arbitrary class already reached, the third the result of applying N to it.
lines.note: This is a specification of a series by base and step. Wittgenstein presents it as saying all that can be said about the form of any proposition at all, which is why 6 is one of the seven main numbered propositions.

lines.f: v(P) = T for every v ∴ P says nothing
lines.d: Tautologies are unconditionally true and therefore convey no information: 4.461, a tautology has no truth conditions, since it is unconditionally true.
lines.note: This is the deflation of logic that the Vienna Circle took over wholesale. Logical truth becomes a degenerate case of the truth-table rather than knowledge of anything.

lines.d: The first failure. Belief is not a truth-function of what is believed: replacing p by a proposition of the same truth value can turn a true belief report into a false one.
lines.note: Wittgenstein saw the objection and answered it at 5.542: 'A believes p' is of the form ' "p" says p ', a correlation of facts and not a relation of a subject to a proposition. Russell, in the 1922 introduction and afterwards, did not accept the answer, and it commits Wittgenstein to a thesis about the self that 5.5421 draws out.

lines.d: The second failure. Generality is treated as a possibly infinite conjunction, which requires that the class the bar covers be specified before N is applied.
lines.note: For an infinite domain no finite sequence of applications specifies it, and the bracket notation gives no mechanism for saying which class is meant. Fogelin (1976) argued that N cannot express mixed multiple generality of the form seen in the Frege entry; Geach (1981) replied with a construction using restricted application, and Soames (1983) pressed the objection again. The dispute is technical and unresolved in the literature.

lines.f: R(a) ∧ Bl(a) = ⊥, yet R(a) and Bl(a) are elementary
lines.d: Colour exclusion. That a point in the visual field is red and that it is blue are incompatible, but on the thesis elementary propositions are logically independent and no contradiction should arise.
lines.note: Tractatus 6.3751 tries to handle the case by analysis into velocities of particles. Wittgenstein withdrew the answer in 'Some Remarks on Logical Form' (1929), the only paper he published after the Tractatus and one he immediately disowned, and by the Philosophical Remarks the independence thesis, and with it line 1, is abandoned.

args.verdict: Sound as a reduction, false as a thesis. Lines 3 and 4 correctly show every finite truth-function generated by N alone. Line 1 is nonetheless false: line 7 exhibits a construction that is not truth-functional, line 8 shows the extension to infinite generality is not secured by the notation offered, and line 9 shows that the elementary propositions the thesis quantifies over are not logically independent as it requires.
args.contested: Whether 5.542 saves the attitude cases is disputed: resolute readers of the Tractatus, Diamond and Conant among them, take the whole apparatus to be deliberately self-undermining and so decline to treat 5.542 as a doctrine at all, while Hacker and the older reading treat it as a substantive and inadequate theory. On the N-operator the technical question is live: Fogelin, Geach and Soames disagree about whether joint negation can express nested quantification, and the answer turns on how much bookkeeping the bar notation may be read as carrying. Wittgenstein's own repudiation is not in doubt.
args.why: Setting the general form beside the two failures shows exactly what kind of claim it is. Lines 3 and 4 are checkable and they hold. Line 7 is a two-line semantic argument that no rewording of the English could deliver, because it turns on substituting one proposition for another of the same truth value, which is only a well-defined operation once truth-functionality has been stated formally. And line 8 shows that the general form is a specification of a series, so that its adequacy is a question about what a series can reach.
args.anachronism: Wittgenstein writes the general form with bars over Greek letters and gives no semantics of valuations; v is imported here to state the failures precisely. Attributing a modern notion of expressive completeness to the N-operator is the very move the Fogelin-Geach dispute is about, so line 8 states a modern question rather than one the Tractatus poses.

args.sub: that what is not cannot be thought or said, so that nothing comes to be and nothing is many
args.work: the poem On Nature, fragments B2, B3, B6, B7 and B8, c. 480 BCE
args.sysn: first-order logic with an explicit existence predicate, used to separate three things the Greek verb keeps together
args.claim: That the second way of inquiry, that it is not, cannot be pursued because what is not can neither be known nor pointed out; and that since coming-to-be and plurality both require what is not, what is must be one, ungenerated, indivisible and unchanging.
key: x is; the existential reading of the Greek verb, deliberately isolated here
a says or points out x
x is F, for an arbitrary predicate F; used to display the predicative reading

lines.d: B2: the way that it is not is wholly unlearnable, for what is not can neither be known nor pointed out.
lines.note: This premise cannot be written without letting the variable range over things that fail E. If the quantifier is read as ranging only over what is, the premise is vacuously true and does no work in the argument.

lines.d: B3, on the usual construal: the same thing is there for thinking and for being. Whatever is thought of, is.
lines.note: The fragment is a single line and its syntax is disputed; the alternative rendering, that thinking and being are the same, gives a much stronger and less usable premise.

lines.d: Whatever is said is thought. B6 forbids saying and thinking the same thing to be and not to be, treating the two together throughout.
Against coming-to-be, B8: what comes to be must previously not have been, and so there would have to be something that is not for it to come from.
lines.note: Lines 1 and 2 then close the case: no such thing could have been thought of or spoken of, so the whole account of generation is unsayable rather than merely false.

lines.d: Against plurality. For two things to be two, each must fail to be the other, and that failure is treated as a case of not-being.
lines.note: Here the conditional is doing all the work, and it is the weakest thing in the argument. Failing to be the other is a denial of identity; it is not the failure of E.

lines.d: What is, is one: ungenerated and imperishable, whole, unique, unmoving and complete, as the signposts of B8 have it.

lines.f: ¬E(x) [x is not at all]   ¬F(x) [x is not F]   x ≠ y [x is not y]
lines.d: Three things the single Greek construction covers. Line 1 needs the first; line 5 supplies only the second or the third.
lines.note: This is the diagnosis Plato makes in the Sophist, at the cost of what he calls parricide against father Parmenides: at 256d-259b not-being is analysed as being other, so that saying what a thing is not is saying what it is different from, and the way of not-being reopens.

lines.f: line 1 is vacuous if ∀ ranges over what satisfies E
lines.d: The regimentation cannot state the ban without breaking it. Either the domain contains what is not, which the conclusion denies, or the premise quantifies over nothing.
lines.note: The dilemma is not a refutation of Parmenides so much as a display of his difficulty: any language with quantifiers and an existence predicate faces it, which is why the problem recurs in Meinong, in Russell's 1905 treatment, and in Quine.

args.verdict: Invalid as regimented, and the notation names the step: line 5 licenses the inference to non-being only if x ≠ y is read as ¬E of something, which line 7 shows it is not. Line 4 is better, and survives if 'is not' is univocal, but it inherits the same equivocation once one asks what the not-yet-existing thing is said not to be. Line 8 shows further that premise 1 cannot be stated in this notation without granting what the conclusion denies.
args.contested: Whether Parmenides commits the confusion at all is genuinely disputed. Owen's 'Eleatic Questions' (1960) gave the existential reading its classic modern statement; the doubts came after it, from Kahn, Furth and Mourelatos. Kahn argued that the Greek einai carries a veridical sense, is the case, which is neither existential nor predicative, so that the modern trichotomy is the wrong instrument. Curd's Legacy of Parmenides (1998) reads the conclusion as predicational rather than numerical monism: not that only one thing exists, but that whatever is has a single unmixed nature, which leaves plurality open and removes the need for line 5. Mourelatos reads the 'is' as speculative predication. On these readings the argument diagnosed here is not the argument in the poem.
args.why: Writing E as a predicate makes the equivocation appear as a mismatch of formulas rather than as a suspicion about a Greek word: line 1 requires ¬E, line 5 delivers only ≠, and no rule connects them. It also exposes something the prose entirely conceals, that the ban on not-being cannot be stated in a quantified language without quantifying over what is not. That is the structural difficulty Plato attacks and that Russell and Quine inherit.
args.anachronism: Parmenides had no quantifiers, no identity sign and no distinction between existence and predication; the Greek verb einai fuses uses that this notation is designed to prise apart, and prising them apart may itself beg the exegetical question. Treating E as a first-order predicate is moreover something Frege and Kant both deny is legitimate, which the god-definition chain takes up.

args.sub: that the firmest of all principles admits of no demonstration, and that its denier can only be refuted out of his own mouth
args.work: Metaphysics Gamma (IV) 3-4, 1005b-1009a, c. 350 BCE
args.sysn: classical propositional logic, with the refutation stated as a condition on assertion rather than as a derivation
args.claim: That the law of non-contradiction is the firmest principle, that it cannot be demonstrated without circularity or regress, and that the denier can nevertheless be refuted, provided only that he says something and means something by it.
key: the property F belongs to the object a
a set of premises offered as a demonstration
the utterance u signifies the property F
x is a man; Aristotle's own example at 1006a31
the law of non-contradiction as stated at line 1

lines.d: Metaphysics 1005b19-20: it is impossible for the same thing to belong and not to belong to the same thing at the same time and in the same respect.
lines.note: The qualifications are not decoration. Aristotle's law is about belonging, so it is an ontological principle first and a semantic or logical one only derivatively; the temporal and respect clauses are what let him accept that things change and that a thing may be pale in one part and not another.

lines.f: Γ ⊢ LNC → LNC is presupposed in asserting Γ
lines.d: 1006a5-11: there is no demonstration of everything, for there would be an infinite regress; to demand a demonstration of this is a want of education.
lines.note: Any premise set offered in support already excludes its own contradictory in being asserted, so the supposed proof either uses the principle it proves or regresses. The indemonstrability claim is the sound half of Gamma 4.

lines.f: D asserts anything → ∃F Sig(D's word, F)
lines.d: 1006a18-22: the starting point is not that the denier grant that something is or is not so, which would beg the question, but only that he signify something, to himself and to another.
lines.note: This is the whole ingenuity of the strategy. Aristotle asks for less than an assertion so as to avoid the circularity of line 2, and then argues that the smaller concession is already enough.

lines.f: Sig(u, F) ∧ Sig(u, G) → F = G
lines.d: To signify one thing. If 'man' signifies two-footed animal, then for anything that is a man, that is what being a man is.
lines.note: Aristotle allows a word to have several definite senses provided they can be numbered and named; what he forbids is a word signifying indefinitely many things, since then it signifies nothing.

lines.d: If the denier lets a word signify a property and its contradictory indifferently, the word marks no difference between anything and anything, and he has said nothing.
lines.note: The argument is that signifying requires excluding. What the denier loses is not truth but content: his utterance fails to divide the cases.

lines.d: The denier is refuted out of his own mouth. In saying anything at all he has used a word that excludes its contradictory, and so has relied on the principle he denies.
lines.note: This is an elenchos and not a demonstration without qualification, though Aristotle's own phrase at 1006a11-12 is that one may demonstrate elenctically. It establishes nothing about how things are; it establishes only that no one can deny the principle in speech. The two are different achievements and the entry turns on not confusing them.

lines.d: 1006a13-15: one who says nothing is, in that respect, like a plant. Against silence there is no argument.
lines.note: Aristotle concedes the limit himself, and the concession is exactly the shape of a refutation as against a proof: it binds the interlocutor, not the world.

lines.f: line 4 ≡ LNC in the theory of signification
lines.d: The charge of circularity, returning at the semantic level. That signifying one thing excludes signifying its contradictory is the law itself, transposed into a theory of meaning.
lines.note: Łukasiewicz pressed this in 1910 and concluded that Aristotle had no adequate proof; Priest (2006) argues that a dialetheist can accept that words signify determinately and still hold that some contradictions are true, so that line 4 is either question-begging or too weak.

args.verdict: The negative half is sound: line 2 correctly shows that any demonstration of the law would beg the question or regress. The positive half is valid but not independent. Line 6 follows from lines 3, 4 and 5, yet line 4 is the disputed step, and line 8 shows that it is the law over again in semantic dress. So the elenchus binds anyone who already treats meaning as exclusion, and no one else.
args.contested: Łukasiewicz's 1910 study is the classical objection: Aristotle offers several arguments in Gamma 4 and none is a proof. Kirwan and Code read the elenchus as intended to be circular in a harmless way, since a first principle can only be defended from what the opponent must do rather than from anything prior. Dialetheists deny the whole framing: Priest holds that some contradictions are true, that the law therefore has counterexamples, and that Gamma 4 conflates the impossibility of asserting a contradiction, which he grants is rare, with its falsity. Whether the qualification 'in the same respect' makes the law unfalsifiable is a further live objection.
args.why: Separating line 2 from line 6 shows two arguments that prose runs together, one about proof and one about assertion, and shows that they have different targets: the first is about what a demonstration can reach, the second about what a speaker can do. Line 7 then makes the shape of an elenchus visible, since a genuine proof would not have an escape by silence. And line 8 puts the circularity charge where it belongs, on a single premise, rather than leaving it as a general suspicion.
args.anachronism: Aristotle has no propositional variables, no distinction between object language and metalanguage, and no notion of a semantic theory; Sig is a modern device for stating what he expresses as talk of what a name signifies. Rendering his ontological principle about belonging as a modal schema over predicates already makes it more like a modern logical law than he takes it to be.

args.sub: that all four of affirmation, denial, both and neither are to be refused, and why that is not simply a rejection of excluded middle
args.work: Mūlamadhyamakakārikā (Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way), especially 1.1, 18.8, 22.11, 24.18-19 and 25.17; c. 150-200 CE
args.sysn: propositional logic, with a presupposition operator on the standard reading and a four-valued semantics on the paraconsistent one
args.claim: That for the questions at issue, whether a thing is real, whether the Buddha exists after death, whether things arise from themselves or another, none of the four available positions may be taken; and that this refusal is a consequence of emptiness rather than a new position alongside the four.
key: an arbitrary proposition, for instance that the Tathāgata exists after death
p is asserted, that is, put forward with commitment
x has svabhāva, intrinsic or own-nature
the premises the opponent has granted, from which the reductio proceeds
the four values of a first-degree entailment semantics: true only, false only, both, neither

lines.d: The four corners, catuṣkoṭi. MMK 18.8 sets them out as everything is real, and is not real, both real and not real, neither real nor not real.
lines.note: The fourth corner is 'neither p nor not-p', which is why it is written as a conjunction of two negations rather than as a third value.

lines.d: Read classically, corners three and four are each contradictory, the fourth by double negation, so the schema collapses into the two corners already listed.
lines.note: This collapse is the problem every interpretation has to solve. If the third and fourth corners are empty the tetralemma is a dilemma with decoration, and the texts plainly treat all four as live.

lines.d: The method is prasaṅga, reduction to absurdity from premises the opponent grants. Nāgārjuna repeatedly says he has no thesis of his own; the Vigrahavyāvartanī 29 makes the disclaimer explicit.
lines.note: If the method yields no commitments, the four corners are being declined rather than denied, and the logical situation is quite different from a denial of excluded middle.

lines.d: The two negations of the Indian grammatical and logical tradition. Commitment-free negation, which merely withholds, against implicative negation, which affirms an alternative.
lines.note: Nothing in Greek or in classical logic corresponds to this distinction, and almost every confused reading of the catuṣkoṭi ignores it. Rejecting p is not asserting not-p.

lines.d: The standard reading. Each corner presupposes that its subject has intrinsic nature; emptiness, argued at 24.18-19 from dependent arising, denies that anything does.
lines.note: On this reading the tetralemma is a presupposition failure, exactly like the classic case of the present king of France, and the four corners fail together because they share a presupposition rather than because any of them is false.

lines.d: All four are declined. Since none is denied, nothing has been asserted whose negation would have to be excluded, and no law of classical logic has been touched.
lines.note: The reading buys consistency at the cost of making the position almost contentless, which is what its critics say and what its defenders regard as the point.

lines.f: v(p) ∈ {t, f, b, n}: corner i = t, ii = f, iii = b, iv = n
lines.d: The paraconsistent reading. On a four-valued semantics the corners are precisely the four values, which explains why there are four and not some other number.
lines.note: Priest and Garfield (2003) take some passages, and the two-truths chapter in particular, to accept true contradictions at the limit of what can be said. Refusing all four then requires a fifth position outside the lattice, which Priest, in The Fifth Corner of Four (2018), treats as the ineffable and models with a plurivalent semantics.

lines.f: standard: ¬A(φ) for all four   paraconsistent: A(iii) for some φ
lines.d: The two readings differ on exactly one question, whether Nāgārjuna ever asserts a contradiction; and the verses do not settle it.
lines.note: The formalisations are both coherent. What is undecided is which one the text supports, and that is a question for philology and for the commentarial tradition, not for logic.

args.verdict: Not one argument but a schema, and on the standard reading it violates no law of classical logic. On the standard reading it is classically consistent: line 5 makes all four corners suffer presupposition failure, and line 4 keeps rejection distinct from denial. On the paraconsistent reading it is deliberately inconsistent but non-trivial, since a paraconsistent consequence relation blocks explosion. The choice between them is exegetical. On the paraconsistent reading, though, first-degree entailment is paracomplete as well as paraconsistent: where a proposition takes the fourth value, neither true nor false, the disjunction of it with its negation is undesignated, so excluded middle lapses. The two readings therefore differ on excluded middle as well as on contradiction.
args.contested: Robinson (1957) argued that Nāgārjuna's logic is classical and that the tetralemma turns on scope and on the opponent's presuppositions. Ruegg (1977) traced the four positions through the commentaries and stressed the prasajya negation. Tillemans (1999) asked whether Buddhist logic is non-classical or merely deviant and answered that it is neither. Against them, Deguchi, Garfield and Priest have defended a dialetheist reading, with Tillemans replying that it reads a modern paraconsistency into texts whose commentators show no sign of it. Different verses support different readings, which is part of why the dispute persists.
args.why: Line 2 makes the interpretive problem sharp rather than atmospheric: in classical logic two of the four corners are simply empty, so any reading that leaves the schema classical owes an account of why there are four. Line 4 then shows where the account comes from, since ¬A(p) and A(¬p) are different formulas and ordinary English has one construction for both. And line 7 shows that the four corners map exactly onto the four values of a familiar non-classical semantics, which is a striking fact and not an argument for the reading.
args.anachronism: Nāgārjuna had a highly developed dialectical practice but no formal language and no semantics; A, Sv and the four values are all imported. The prasajya distinction is genuinely his tradition's, but stating it as a scope difference between an operator and a connective is modern. Whether four-valued semantics illuminates the verses or merely re-describes them in a congenial notation is precisely what the Priest-Tillemans dispute is about.

args.n: Dialectic is not a rule of inference
args.sub: that the schema attributed to Hegel is neither his own nor, taken as a rule, a rule at all
args.work: Science of Logic, 1812-16, revised 1832; Encyclopaedia Logic, 1830, especially section 79
args.sysn: no formal system: the lines set out the schema commonly attributed and the reasons it is not an inference rule
args.claim: That the transitions of the Logic are not instances of any inference rule; that the thesis-antithesis-synthesis formula is not Hegel's; and that Aufhebung cannot be a truth-functional operation, because its defining work is on content rather than on truth value.
key: the thesis, in the received schema
the supposed operation of Aufhebung applied to two propositions
the four assignments of truth values to an ordered pair of propositions

lines.d: The schema as it is commonly attributed: a thesis, its opposite, and a synthesis that resolves them. This is the thing to be examined, not a premise Hegel supplies.

lines.f: the schema at line 1 is not Hegel's vocabulary
lines.d: The triad belongs to Fichte and to the reception. Chalybaus popularised it as a summary of Hegel in 1837, six years after Hegel's death.
lines.note: Mueller's 'The Hegel Legend of Thesis-Antithesis-Synthesis' (1958) argued that Hegel uses the three words together only once, and there to describe Kant. Hegel's own triad, at Encyclopaedia section 79, is the abstract or understanding side, the dialectical or negatively rational side, and the speculative or positively rational side.

lines.d: Taken as a classical inference rule, line 1 is not a rule but a licence. From a contradiction everything follows, so the schema would sanction any synthesis whatever.
lines.note: Making it non-explosive requires a paraconsistent consequence relation, which is a substantive logical commitment the schema does not state and which Hegel is in no position to have made.

lines.f: there is no f: {T, F}² → {T, F} answering to Auf
lines.d: There are sixteen binary truth-functions. Aufheben must cancel its argument, preserve it, and raise it at once, the triple sense Hegel remarks on in the German word after the transition to Becoming.
lines.note: The reason is not that the right function has yet to be found. A truth-function returns a truth value, and preservation of content is not something a truth value can record; the operation and the value space are of different kinds.

lines.d: The first transition of the Logic. Being and Nothing are each wholly indeterminate, each passes into the other, and their truth is Becoming.
lines.note: The determinate negation is the negation of a content, not of a truth value, and its result is a specific further content rather than a complement. Nothing is not the contradictory of Being, and Becoming is not any Boolean combination of the two, which is why the transition cannot be an instance of line 1.

lines.f: T is untrue once S is reached ∴ not (T ⊨ S)
lines.d: The earlier category is declared untrue in Hegel's sense, inadequate to its own concept, and yet retained as a moment of what follows.
lines.note: A consequence relation requires that the truth of the premises guarantee the truth of the conclusion. A movement that gives up its starting point while keeping it is not that relation, whatever else it is.

lines.f: partial formalisations exist; none derives the order of the categories
lines.d: Kosok (1966) offered a formalisation of the dialectical structure; Priest ('Dialectic and Dialetheic', 1989) reconstructed parts of Hegel paraconsistently; there are category-theoretic and modal attempts since.
lines.note: Each captures a fragment, and Priest's in particular makes good sense of Hegel's claim that all things are in themselves contradictory. None reproduces the sequence of the Logic, because what fixes the order of the categories is their content, and no formal apparatus supplies content.

lines.f: there is no rule R such that the transitions of the Logic are instances of R
lines.d: The received schema is a misattribution, and no assignment of a truth-function or a rule makes it a rule. This is a claim about the limits of the formal layer, and it is the reason the entry is here.
lines.note: Nothing in this shows that Hegel is confused, only that whatever the Logic is doing is not inference in the sense the rest of this chain uses. Where the demonstration fails is where the exercise ends.

args.verdict: The received schema is a misattribution, as line 2 records, and as a rule it is defective twice over: line 3 shows it explosive if read classically, and line 4 shows that its operator cannot be defined truth-functionally at all. Hegel's actual transitions are not instances of it, as line 5 shows for the first of them. The correct verdict is not that the argument is invalid but that there is no argument of the required kind to assess.
args.contested: Whether Hegel's dialectic can be formalised at all divides the literature. Priest and Routley held that Hegel is a dialetheist whose claim that things are contradictory should be taken at face value and rendered in a paraconsistent logic; Inwood and most Hegel scholars reply that Widerspruch in the Logic is not the contradiction of formal logic but the instability of a determination that undermines itself, so that paraconsistency answers a question Hegel does not ask. Whether the Logic's order is necessary or merely presented as such is separately disputed, and it decides whether a formal reconstruction could even be the right ambition.
args.why: The notation earns its keep here by failing in a specific way. Line 3 shows that anyone treating the schema as a rule has committed to a paraconsistent consequence relation without saying so; line 4 shows why Aufhebung is not a connective, by counting the available functions and noting that none of them can preserve what it cancels; and line 6 shows that the movement does not even have the shape of a consequence relation, since its premises are surrendered. Marking that boundary is a result about the formal layer.
args.anachronism: The whole entry is an anachronism by design. Hegel wrote before the mathematical logic that supplies truth-functions and consequence relations, and he regarded the formal logic he knew as precisely the abstraction the Logic was meant to overcome. Judging him by whether his transitions are instances of a rule is judging him by a standard he rejected, and the entry claims only that the standard cannot be met, not that it should govern.

args.n: That than which nothing greater can be conceived
args.sub: that grasping the description of God commits you to his existing outside the mind
args.work: Proslogion II, 1077-78
args.sysn: first-order logic with a comparative relation ranging over merely conceived objects as well as real ones
args.claim: That anyone who understands the phrase that than which nothing greater can be conceived is committed on pain of contradiction to holding that such a being exists in reality and not only in the understanding.
key: x is a being than which nothing greater can be conceived
the individual assumed at line 4 to be G and to exist in the understanding alone

lines.d: Even the fool who denies God hears the phrase and understands it; what is understood is in the understanding. So something answering to the description is in the understanding.
lines.note: The whole argument turns on reading this with the quantifier outside: there is an object which is G and which is in the understanding. The weaker and more natural reading, that the fool grasps a concept, has no object in it at all, and yields nothing later.

lines.d: To be that than which nothing greater can be conceived is for nothing conceivable whatever to be greater. The quantifier is unrestricted across everything conceivable.
lines.note: Note that the bound variable y ranges over conceivable things, not over existing things. Anselm needs this, because at line 5 the greater thing is produced by conceiving it.

lines.d: Whatever is in the understanding alone is such that something greater can be conceived, namely a thing otherwise like it that also exists in reality. Real existence makes a thing greater.
lines.note: This is the load-bearing premise. It requires that Gr compare an item that does not exist with an item that does, so the domain must contain non-existents and the comparison must cross the divide.

lines.d: Assume for reductio that the being than which nothing greater can be conceived is in the understanding but not in reality, which is what the fool's denial amounts to.
From lines 3 and 4 by universal instantiation and modus ponens: something conceivable is greater than a.
From lines 2 and 4: since a is G, nothing conceivable is greater than a.
Lines 5 and 6 are contradictory. The assumption at line 4 is discharged, giving that anything both G and in the understanding exists in reality.

Combining the discharged conditional with line 1: that than which nothing greater can be conceived exists in reality as well as in the understanding. Proslogion III then adds that it cannot be conceived not to exist.

args.verdict: Formally valid as a reductio. Everything therefore rests on lines 1, 2 and 3, and the notation shows they cannot all be read the same way at once: line 1 needs a genuine object in the domain, line 3 needs that object to be comparable with a real one, and line 2 needs the comparison class to include things that do not exist.
args.contested: Aquinas denies line 1 outright (Summa Theologiae I q.2 a.1): the description gives no quid est we grasp, so nothing enters the understanding as an object. Kant attacks line 3, since it treats real existence as a great-making feature an object can lack. Twentieth-century readers split on the domain: Barnes and others treat Anselm as quantifying over a Meinongian range of objects some of which fail to exist, while Klima and Adams argue that his esse in intellectu is a mode of being a thing has qua thought of, which is not the same commitment. Validity is the one thing this reconstruction is rarely challenged on, though Oppy and others deny that any valid reconstruction is faithful to the chapter.
args.why: The English hides two shifts. First, moving from the fool understanding a phrase to a thing being in his understanding is a quantifier shift, and the argument survives only on the stronger reading. Second, once written out, line 3's ∃y is seen to range over conceived and unconceived objects alike, so Gr must relate a non-existent to an existent. Symbolised, the argument's price is a domain of merely conceived objects, which the Latin never has to admit aloud.
args.anachronism: Anselm had no quantifier, no variable-binding, and no explicit domain. The choice of domain is the reconstruction's decision, not his, and scholars disagree about whether attributing a Meinongian domain to him is illuminating or a distortion of esse in intellectu.

args.sub: that Anselm's schema, applied to an island, proves an island
args.work: Pro Insipiente (On Behalf of the Fool), c. 1078
args.sysn: first-order logic, with Anselm's reasoning treated as a schema open to substitution for a kind-term
args.claim: That the pattern of inference used in Proslogion II, applied without alteration to the greatest conceivable island, yields the existence of that island, and therefore that the pattern is unsound.
key: x is a K, where K is a schematic kind-term to be substituted
x is a K than which no greater K can be conceived

lines.d: Generalise Anselm's definition by leaving the kind open: M holds of whatever is a K such that no conceivable K is greater. Anselm's own case is K taken as being.

This is the Proslogion II derivation with the kind left schematic. It is valid for every substitution for K, since the derivation turns only on the uniform occurrence of K and never on what kind of thing K is.
lines.note: That the derivation nowhere uses the content of K is the entire parody. A schema-substitution objection does not dispute a premise; it exhibits an instance.

lines.d: Substitute: let K be the predicate is an island. M now reads: the island than which no greater island can be conceived, blessed with untold riches.
I have heard the phrase and understood it, exactly as the fool understood Anselm's. So the Lost Island is in my understanding.
lines.note: The instance of line 1 of Proslogion II. If this is true for the phrase Anselm uses, it is hard to see why it is false for this one.

lines.d: By the rule at line 2, applied to the substitution instance: the Lost Island exists somewhere in the ocean.
No such island exists. Gaunilo takes this as evident, and Anselm never disputes it.
Lines 5 and 6 are contradictory. Since the rule at line 2 is valid, some premise of the schema must fail, and it must fail in Anselm's instance too unless a difference is shown.

args.verdict: The parody is formally correct: the derivation is genuinely schematic, so if it is sound for one substitution it is sound for all unless a premise fails at the substitution. That last clause is Anselm's escape, and it is a real one, so the parody refutes the argument only in the absence of a reply.
args.contested: Anselm's Reply 3 grants the island but denies the instance: only for that than which nothing greater can be conceived does the definition itself entail that it cannot be conceived not to exist, so only there does the greater-making premise bite. Two defences of the reply are current. One, from Plantinga (1974), is that greatest conceivable island is unsatisfiable even in the understanding, since island-greatness has no intrinsic maximum: another palm tree is always conceivable, so line 4 is false. The other, from Malcolm and Hartshorne, is that necessary existence attaches only to a being whose non-existence is inconceivable. Oppy (1995) replies that the maximum can be stipulated away. Anselm's own emphasis in Reply 3 is read differently by some: he denies that the Proslogion argument rests on any general principle that a thing is greater for existing in reality, and on that account there is no schema for Gaunilo to instantiate and so no rejoinder owed to the island in particular. Whether the reply concedes the schema and blocks the substitution, or refuses the schema outright, is itself disputed. The island is also only part of the reply. Gaunilo's leading charge is epistemic: that the fool cannot form the thought of that than which nothing greater can be conceived as an object at all, so that nothing enters his understanding — an attack on line 4 rather than on the rule at line 2.
args.why: Writing Proslogion II as a schema with a free kind-letter makes the objection and the reply both precise, and shows that they are not in conflict. The notation locates Gaunilo's charge at the rule and Anselm's reply at the premise, which is why each side could feel it had won. It also shows what a successful reply must do: not defend the inference, which is valid for any K, but exhibit a premise that fails when K is island and holds when K is being.

args.sub: that existence belongs to the idea of a supremely perfect being as three angles belong to the idea of a triangle
args.work: Meditationes de prima philosophia, Meditation V, 1641
args.sysn: second-order logic, quantifying over perfections, with existence written as one first-order predicate among them
args.claim: That existence is contained in the idea of a supremely perfect being as inseparably as having angles equal to two right angles is contained in the idea of a triangle, and that a supremely perfect being therefore exists.
key: x is a supremely perfect being
x has angles equal to two right angles

lines.d: A supremely perfect being is one having every perfection. The quantifier over f is second-order: it ranges over properties, and Perf sorts them.
Existence is a perfection. A thing that exists is to that extent more perfect than one that does not, so E belongs on the list of properties Perf collects.
lines.note: Here existence is being treated as a first-order predicate, on all fours with omniscience and omnipotence. This is precisely the step Kant will refuse.

lines.d: From lines 1 and 2: anything that is supremely perfect exists. Existence can no more be separated from the idea of God than a valley from a mountain.
The analogy Descartes offers: whatever I clearly and distinctly perceive to belong to the nature of a triangle does belong to every triangle, whether or not any triangle exists.
lines.note: The analogy is exact, and that is the difficulty. Line 4 has the form of line 3 and is compatible with there being no triangles at all.

lines.d: Consistent. A universally quantified conditional is vacuously true when nothing satisfies its antecedent, so line 3 is likewise consistent with nothing being supremely perfect.
The needed and unstated further premise: the idea of a supremely perfect being is a true and immutable nature rather than a fiction, so such a being is at least possible.
Descartes takes lines 3 and 6 to give the conclusion: a nature that contains existence cannot be merely possible, so a supremely perfect being exists.

args.verdict: Invalid as it stands, at line 7. Lines 3 and 6 give only ◇∃x S(x), and the passage from possible instantiation to actual instantiation requires a modal principle Descartes states only obliquely, in the First Replies, as the claim that the idea of God contains necessary and not merely possible existence. Supplying that principle is exactly what the twentieth-century modal version does.
args.contested: Leibniz, who saw the argument in 1676 and wrote Quod ens perfectissimum existit for Spinoza, accepted the structure but insisted line 6 needs proof: one must show that the perfections are jointly consistent, since a concept that harbours a contradiction has no true and immutable nature. His demonstration, that perfections are simple positive qualities and so cannot conflict, is generally judged unsuccessful. Caterus in the First Objections had already pressed the vacuity point behind line 5, and Gassendi in the Fifth Objections denied line 2 directly, holding that existence is not a property of anything. A further dispute is whether the argument is an inference at all. Descartes tells his objectors that the conclusion is grasped in a single clear and distinct perception rather than reached by syllogism, and readers who take that seriously hold that supplying a missing premise misdescribes the argument rather than repairing it.
args.why: Setting the triangle beside the deity in the same notation shows that the analogy is fatal rather than helpful. Both come out as universally quantified conditionals, and the triangle case is the standard textbook example of one that is compatible with an empty extension. The symbols also expose the missing possibility premise at line 6, which the prose smuggles in under true and immutable nature, and they display existence sitting inside a second-order list of perfections, which is the exact configuration Kant will declare ill-formed.
args.anachronism: The second-order quantifier over perfections is a regimentation of scholastic talk of attributa, and the isolation of line 6 as a separate premise is due to Leibniz rather than to Descartes, who thought the possibility self-evident from clear and distinct perception.

args.n: Being is not a real predicate
args.sub: that existence is what the quantifier does, and so cannot be part of what a concept says
args.work: Kritik der reinen Vernunft A592/B620-A602/B630, 1781 and 1787
args.sysn: first-order logic with the existential quantifier, set against a second-level reading of existence as a property of concepts
args.claim: That existence adds nothing to the content of any concept, so that no analysis of the concept of God, however complete, can yield the proposition that God exists.
key: x has the divine perfections, that is, x falls under the concept of the most real being
x exists, taken as the ontological argument takes it, as a first-order predicate
an arbitrary individual of the domain

lines.d: What the ontological argument must deliver, and the form in which it needs E: a predicate that a concept can contain and that an object can be said to satisfy.
lines.note: Kant's target is the conjunction. If E is a predicate at all like G, then G(x) ∧ E(x) should be a richer concept than G(x).

lines.d: Spell out the first-order predicate. To say that a exists is to say that something in the domain is identical with a, and nothing more.
In classical first-order logic, with a non-empty domain and every name denoting, this is valid. E holds of everything whatever, so it distinguishes no object from any other.
lines.note: Line 4 below is the formal rendering of the hundred thalers: the real hundred contain not one coin more than the possible hundred.

lines.d: Adding existence to a concept yields a logically equivalent concept. So no concept is enlarged by writing existence into it, and none is defective for leaving it out.
Frege's regimentation in the Grundlagen of 1884: existence is a second-level predicate, something said of a concept, namely that it is instantiated, not a mark of the objects falling under it.
Descartes' second line is now ill-formed. Perf takes first-level concepts as arguments; existence, being second-level, is not among the things Perf can sort.
lines.note: The two lines of attack are distinct: line 3 says E is trivial, line 6 says E is not that kind of item at all. Kant is usually read as making the first point, Frege as making the second.

lines.d: The conditional the ontological argument establishes is a logical truth and settles nothing. Whether the concept of the most real being is instantiated remains open, and no analysis can close it.

args.verdict: The diagnosis is correct given classical first-order logic with a total domain, and it holds against both Anselm's line 3 and Descartes' line 2. It does not touch an argument that never treats existence as a first-order predicate, which is why the modal version escapes it.
args.contested: Two disputes. First, whether Frege's thesis is Kant's: Kant grants that being is a logical predicate while denying it is a real or determining one, which is a point about positing rather than about levels, and Bennett, Wiggins and Forgie have read the two as substantially different. Second, whether line 3 is a truth of logic or an artefact of the logic chosen: in free logic, existence is a first-order predicate and E(a) is not valid, so the objection has to be remade there. Defenders of the argument, including Plantinga, therefore regard the Kantian objection as decisive only against the Cartesian formulation.
args.why: This is the clearest case on the site of a modern notation vindicating an eighteenth-century objection. Kant's claim reads in prose as a piece of rhetoric about thalers, and in symbols it becomes a theorem: ∀x E(x) is valid, so E partitions nothing. The two-level display then shows why the ontological argument is not merely unsound but malformed: it feeds a second-level predicate into a first-level slot, and no repair of its premises can fix that.
args.anachronism: Kant had no quantifier and no distinction of levels; both are Frege's, from 1879 and 1884. He had made the same claim already in Der einzig mögliche Beweisgrund of 1763, in terms of positing rather than predication, and whether that earlier formulation is the same objection is itself disputed.

args.sub: that if a maximally great being is possible then, in S5, it is actual
args.work: Malcolm, Anselm's Ontological Arguments, 1960; Plantinga, The Nature of Necessity, 1974 ; Hartshorne, The Logic of Perfection, 1962
args.sysn: propositional modal logic S5, in which possible necessity collapses into necessity
args.claim: That the existence of a maximally great being is either impossible or necessary, so that its mere possibility suffices for its actuality, given the S5 principle that what is possibly necessary is necessary.
key: x is maximally excellent: omniscient, omnipotent and morally perfect
the proposition that a maximally great being exists

lines.d: Maximal greatness is maximal excellence in every possible world. So the proposition g, that a maximally great being exists, is itself world-indexed to all worlds.
lines.note: Existence is not being treated as a perfection here. What does the work is the modal profile of the property, which is why Kant's objection does not engage this version.

lines.d: Immediate from line 1: if greatness is possessed in every world, then in every world it is possessed, so g holds necessarily if it holds at all.
The possibility premise. There is some possible world in which a maximally great being exists. This is presented as the modest claim, and it is the only substantive one.
From lines 2 and 3 by the K axiom and necessitation on line 2: since g entails its own necessity, a world in which g holds is a world in which g is necessary.
The characteristic S5 principle, equivalent to the axiom that possibility is necessary. It holds when accessibility is an equivalence relation, and fails in K, T and S4.
From lines 4 and 5, g is necessary; from the T axiom that necessity implies truth, a maximally great being exists in the actual world.
The parody, move for move. Lines 2 and 5 give ◇g → g, whose contrapositive is that non-existence is necessary if it holds at all, so the atheist's ◇□¬g yields □¬g by the same axiom.
lines.note: Both premises look modest and they are contradictory, which shows that neither is modest. In S5 line 3 is already equivalent to the conclusion.

args.verdict: Valid in S5, and Plantinga does not claim more. All the weight has moved to line 3, and line 7 shows that line 3 is not the small concession it appears to be: given line 2, ◇g and g are equivalent, so anyone who grants the possibility premise has granted the conclusion.
args.contested: Three disputes. Whether S5 is the right logic for metaphysical modality: most now think it is, though the transitivity axiom has been questioned by Salmon and others for de re essentialist cases. Whether line 3 can be supported without begging the question: Plantinga himself concluded that the argument shows rational acceptability rather than proves its conclusion, and Mackie (1982) and Oppy (1995) hold that the symmetric parody at line 7 leaves the two possibility claims in stalemate. And whether the concept of maximal greatness is coherent at all, which is line 3 read as a consistency claim.
args.why: The formalisation does one decisive thing: it shows exactly where the argument's work is done. In prose the modal version looks like a strengthening of Anselm, with more machinery and therefore more force. In symbols the machinery at lines 4 to 6 turns out to be an inference nobody disputes, and everything hangs on line 3, which the parody at line 7 matches step for step. The notation converts an argument about God into a question about who bears the burden on a bare possibility claim.
args.anachronism: Anselm had no possible worlds and no modal operators. Malcolm, Hartshorne and Barth read Proslogion III, where Anselm says God cannot be conceived not to exist, as a second and modal argument distinct from Proslogion II; most scholars regard that as a modern imposition on a passage that is more plausibly a corollary of the reductio, and the question is genuinely disputed.

args.sub: that whatever is merely possible in itself requires something necessary in itself
args.work: Kitab al-Shifa', al-Ilahiyyat I.6-7, c. 1020s; al-Isharat wa-l-Tanbihat IV, c. 1030
args.sysn: first-order logic with an essence operator and an entailment relation between essence and existence
args.claim: That every existing thing is either necessary through itself or possible through itself, that nothing possible through itself can account for its own existence, and that there is therefore a necessary existent.
key: the essence or quiddity of x, considered in itself
y is that through which x exists, the preponderator that tips x into existence
the totality of existing things that are possible in themselves

lines.d: A thing is necessary in itself when its existence follows from what it is. Its essence and its existence are not two, so it needs nothing else to exist.
lines.note: This is the essence-existence distinction stated formally. For every other thing existence is an addition to the quiddity, which is the doctrine Aquinas takes over as the real distinction.

lines.d: A thing is possible in itself when its quiddity, taken alone, settles neither that it exists nor that it does not. Horseness considered as such is neither existent nor non-existent.
The division is exhaustive and exclusive over what exists. Things impossible in themselves do not exist at all, so every existent falls on exactly one side.
Whatever is possible in itself but does exist has been made necessary by another. Something distinct from it must tip the balance, since its own essence leaves the matter open.
lines.note: The clause y ≠ x carries the whole prohibition on self-causation, and it is what generates the contradiction at line 7.

lines.d: Assume for reductio that there is no necessary existent, so that everything that exists is merely possible in itself.
Take t, the totality of existing possibles. By the assumption t is itself possible in itself, so by line 4 something other than t makes it exist.
lines.note: The step from every member being P to the aggregate being P is the aggregation move. Whether a totality is the kind of thing that has an essence at all is the point Hume and Russell later press.

lines.d: Either y belongs to t, in which case it causes the whole that contains it and so causes itself, contradicting line 4; or it lies outside t, in which case it is not possible, contradicting line 5.
Discharging line 5: there is a necessary existent. Avicenna then argues separately that it is unique, simple, and identical with its own existence.

args.verdict: Valid given lines 3, 4 and the aggregation step at line 6. The disputed premise is line 6, and specifically the treatment of t as an object with a quiddity to which lines 2 and 4 apply.
args.contested: Whether Avicenna needs the totality at all is disputed. Marmura (1980) reconstructs the Shifa' proof as running from Ilahiyyat I.6 through VIII.1-3 and as resting on the impossibility of an infinite chain of concurrent causes rather than on an aggregate, whereas the Isharat and the Najat do take the totality of caused things and canvass the ways its existence might be accounted for, so line 6 formalises those works rather than the Shifa' chapters cited above. Al-Ghazali attacked the doctrine of a necessary existent whose act is eternal, not the division at line 3, which Ash'arite theology largely accepted. Averroes objected that the argument is metaphysical where it should be physical, and Aquinas adopted lines 1 and 2 while rejecting the aggregate step in favour of a regress claim. The argument is known as the burhān al-ṣiddīqīn, the demonstration of the veracious, a name Avicenna himself uses when he remarks at the end of the Isharat that this way of proceeding takes nothing but existence itself for its middle term; the title was fixed as a label by the later tradition, and Mulla Sadra later claimed it for a version of his own.
args.why: The prose formula that God's essence is his existence is easy to read as pious paradox. Written as an entailment between the essence operator and the existence predicate, it becomes a definition that does work: line 1 states the property, line 2 states its negation, and line 3 shows the two are jointly exhaustive over what exists, which is what makes the reductio possible. The notation also isolates the aggregation step at line 6, which the Arabic conceals under the word for totality.
args.anachronism: The entailment sign between an essence and an existence predicate is a modern device; Avicenna's terms are wujub, imkan and murajjih, and his logic is Aristotelian syllogistic with no quantifier over totalities.

args.sub: that the past cannot be an actual infinite, so the universe began and had a cause
args.work: Tahafut al-Falasifa, Discussion 1, 1095; al-Iqtisad fi al-I'tiqad, c. 1095
args.sysn: first-order logic with a cardinality comparison over completed collections
args.claim: That the series of past events cannot be an actual infinite, that the universe therefore began to exist, and that it therefore has a cause of its beginning.
key: y is a cause of x's beginning
S is an actual infinite: a completed collection with infinitely many members
the number of members of S
S' is a proper part of S
the completed series of the sun's past revolutions
the completed series of Saturn's past revolutions

lines.d: Whatever begins to exist has a cause of its beginning. Al-Ghazali takes this as evident: what comes to be at one moment rather than another needs something to determine that.
The universe began to exist. This is the premise the philosophers denied, holding the world eternal, and it is what the sub-argument at lines 4 to 7 is for.
From lines 1 and 2 by instantiation and modus ponens. The main argument is a single application of modus ponens and holds no logical interest whatever.
