The whole is greater than the part, Euclid's fifth common notion, applied to completed collections. This is the hinge of the whole argument, and it is never stated as a premise.
lines.note: The pairing at line 6 is what makes Sat a proper part of Sun. Al-Ghazali treats the axiom as a truth of reason needing no defence, which in 1095 it was.

lines.d: Actual infinites do not differ in magnitude: one infinite cannot be greater or smaller than another, since an infinite is that beyond which there is nothing further to count.
Suppose the past beginningless. Then both revolution-series are completed infinites, and Saturn has made one revolution for every thirty of the sun's, so its series pairs with a proper part.
Line 4 gives the inequality, line 5 the identity. Discharging line 6 yields B(u), which is line 2, and the argument closes.
Dedekind's 1888 definition, which makes the very property al-Ghazali treats as absurd into the definition of infinity. Line 4 is thereby denied for infinite collections, and with it line 7.

args.verdict: The main argument at lines 1 to 3 is valid and trivial. The sub-argument is valid too, and turns entirely on line 4. Since Cantor and Dedekind, line 4 is false of sets, so the argument survives only if line 4 can be defended for concrete collections while being abandoned for abstract ones.
args.contested: That restriction is exactly the modern debate. Craig (1979) revives the argument by holding that Cantorian arithmetic is a consistent formal system with no application to concrete collections, so that Euclidean part-whole comparison remains a constraint on real series of events; Mackie (1982), Sobel (2004) and Oppy (2006) reply that no independent ground has been given for the restriction, and that Hilbert's hotel is strange rather than contradictory. A separate line of attack targets line 1: Hume's Treatise I.iii.3 denies that the causal principle is knowable a priori, and Quantum cosmologists dispute it for the initial state. The sub-argument is inherited rather than invented. John Philoponus turned the impossibility of an actual infinite against Aristotle's eternal world in the sixth century, and the argument had passed through the mutakallimun to al-Kindi, whose proof of the finitude of past time is the same one, and to Saadia Gaon, well before the Tahafut. What is al-Ghazali's is the sharpness of the celestial-revolutions case, not the axiom it rests on.
args.why: The formalisation earns its place by showing that the famous three-line syllogism is not the argument. Setting line 4 out as an explicit axiom, which no medieval statement of the argument sets down as a premise of it, identifies the single proposition on which the case rests and shows that it is not a premise about God, or the universe, or causation, but a claim about the arithmetic of completed collections. Placing Dedekind's definition at line 8 shows the collision precisely: what al-Ghazali offers as a reductio is now the definition of the thing he thought he had refuted.
args.anachronism: Al-Ghazali had no cardinal arithmetic and no notion of one-to-one correspondence; the pairing of Saturn's revolutions with a proper part of the sun's is a modern way of putting an argument he states in terms of one number being greater than another. The name by which the argument now travels is also modern: kalam cosmological argument is Craig's coinage from 1979, applied retrospectively to a family of arguments the mutakallimun themselves did not group under a title.

args.sub: that a series of causes each sustaining the next cannot be endless
args.work: Summa Theologiae I q.2 a.3, c. 1265-68
args.sysn: first-order logic with a well-foundedness condition imposed on a causal relation
args.claim: That in any order of efficient causes in which each intermediate causes only by being here and now caused, there must be a first cause, since removing the first removes the effect.
key: x is here and now the efficient cause of y's causing
a function from the natural numbers into the causal series
x begets y, an accidentally ordered cause

lines.d: The relation is a per se or essentially ordered one: the hand moves the staff which moves the stone, all at once, and the staff moves only while the hand does.
lines.note: Everything in the argument depends on this line, and it is the line popular treatments drop. C is not the relation of an earlier event to a later one.

lines.d: Nothing is the efficient cause of itself, since it would then be prior to itself, which is impossible. Aquinas states this as the argument's first move.
Whatever is caused has a cause. This is a definition rather than a discovery; the substantive claim is that the things we observe are caused in this way.
No infinite descending chain under C: equivalently, every non-empty per se ordered series has a member x with no y in the series such that C(y,x). The relation is well-founded.
lines.note: Well-foundedness is the exact content of removing the first removes the effect. In a series where each member's causing is borrowed, an endless series is one in which nothing has causal power to lend.

lines.d: The minimality form of line 4, applied to any actual per se series: it terminates upwards in a member that causes without being caused to cause.
There is a first efficient cause, to which everyone gives the name of God. The identification is a naming, not a further step of the proof.
Aquinas explicitly allows this: an endless accidentally ordered series, a man begotten by a man begotten by a man, involves no contradiction, and the world's beginning in time cannot be demonstrated.
lines.note: Stated at ST I q.46 a.2 and argued at length in De aeternitate mundi, 1271. Aquinas held the world's beginning on faith and denied it was provable, which places him against al-Ghazali on exactly this point.

args.verdict: Valid. The disputed premise is line 4, and only for the relation defined at line 1. The argument does not conclude that there is one first cause for all series, only that each per se series has a first member; the uniqueness is argued separately at ST I q.11.
args.contested: Line 4 is contested in two ways. Some, following Scotus's refinement in Ordinatio I d.2, hold that the per se ordering makes well-foundedness analytic, since a member with only borrowed causal power in an endless series has none to borrow. Others, from Mackie (1982) to Oppy (2006), reply that this presupposes that causal power is transmitted rather than exercised, and that a series with no first member may simply be a series in which every member's causing is explained by its predecessor with nothing left over. A third question is whether any actual causal series is per se ordered at all, given that contemporary physics offers no simultaneous sustaining causation. A prior question is textual. The Second Way as Aquinas writes it at q.2 a.3 says only that there is an order of efficient causes in which none is prior to itself and the first is cause of the intermediate; it contains neither the words per se and per accidens nor any simultaneity condition. Line 1 is drawn from elsewhere in the corpus, chiefly q.46 a.2 ad 7 and the commentary on the Physics, and readers who take the distinction to be absent from the Second Way read it as an argument about causal order simply.
args.why: The notation fixes the one thing popular presentations always lose. Writing line 1 as a simultaneity condition and line 4 as well-foundedness makes visible that the regress denied is a structural condition on a relation, not a claim about the age of the world, and line 7 records that Aquinas expressly permitted an infinite past. The formalisation also shows that line 6 delivers a first member per series, not a single first cause, so the step to monotheism is not in this argument.
args.anachronism: Well-foundedness is a nineteenth-century set-theoretic notion, and writing line 4 with a function on the naturals imports an apparatus Aquinas would not recognise; his own argument is that in any ordered series removing the first removes the rest.

args.n: Sufficient reason and the contingent series
args.sub: that the series of contingent things, however long, does not contain its own reason
args.work: De rerum originatione radicali, 1697; Monadologie 31-38, 1714
args.sysn: propositional modal logic, with quantification over propositions; only the K rule that necessity is closed under entailment is needed
args.claim: That every truth has a sufficient reason, that no contingent truth or collection of them can be its own sufficient reason, and that the reason for the whole contingent world therefore lies in a necessary being outside it.
key: q is a sufficient reason for p
p is contingent: possibly true and possibly false
the conjunction of all contingent truths
q is a conjunct of c

lines.d: The principle of sufficient reason: nothing is so without there being a reason why it is so and not otherwise. Leibniz calls it, with the law of contradiction, one of the two great principles.
lines.note: Note the unrestricted quantifier. Restricting it to contingent truths, or to truths of a certain kind, is the standard modern retreat and it costs the argument its generality.

lines.d: A contingent truth is one whose contradictory implies no contradiction: the world contains many, since God might have chosen otherwise.
Let c be the conjunction of every contingent truth. A conjunction of contingent truths is itself contingent, since a world in which any conjunct fails is a world in which c fails.
From line 1 applied to c. The whole series of contingent things, however far back it is traced, must have a sufficient reason.
No conjunct is a sufficient reason for the conjunction that contains it, since it would then be part of what it explains. So the reason for c is not contingent, hence necessary.
The sufficient reason of the contingent series lies outside the series, in a being whose reason for existing is in itself: an ultimate reason of things, which Leibniz calls God.
If explaining is entailing, then a necessary reason for c necessitates c, and c was stipulated contingent. Every contingent truth collapses into a necessary one and line 3 is false.

args.verdict: Valid down to line 6, and line 7 is valid too, which is the difficulty: the same principles yield both the conclusion and its refutation. Something must go, and the three candidates are line 1, the identification of explanation with entailment at line 7, and the contingency of c at line 3.
args.contested: Line 7 is van Inwagen's argument (An Essay on Free Will, 1983, pp. 202-4), made independently a year later by Bennett (A Study of Spinoza's Ethics, 1984, pp. 114-16) and related to Spinoza's necessitarianism; Rowe (1975) had pressed a neighbouring objection. Pruss (2006) defends the principle by denying that sufficient reasons must entail, so that a free choice explains without necessitating; Della Rocca (2010) goes the other way, pressing the demand for explicability and accepting its consequences rather than softening them. That is Leibniz's own escape: reasons incline without necessitating, and God's choice of the best is morally rather than metaphysically necessary. The cost is that it is then unclear in what sense the reason is sufficient. Hume's separate objection, that once each member of the series is explained the whole needs no further explanation, attacks line 3 and line 5 together.
args.why: In prose the principle of sufficient reason sounds like a maxim of good intellectual manners, and the objection to it sounds like pedantry. Written out, line 1 is an unrestricted axiom and line 7 is three lines of modal logic requiring nothing stronger than K: necessity is closed under entailment, so a necessary reason that entails c makes c necessary. The notation shows that the price of the argument is the abolition of contingency, and shows that the only exits are to weaken the axiom or to deny that explanation entails.
args.anachronism: Leibniz has no distinction between entailment and explanation to lose, and the conjunction of all contingent truths as a single object of explanation is a twentieth-century device from Rowe and van Inwagen rather than a Leibnizian one.

args.sub: that the argument from order is an analogy, and a weak one at every joint
args.work: Dialogues concerning Natural Religion, Parts II, V, VII and XII, written from 1751, published 1779
args.sysn: informal: an argument from analogy, whose schema is displayed rather than derived, since analogical inference has no valid form to violate
args.claim: That the inference from the order of the world to an intelligent designer is an argument from analogy whose strength varies with the resemblance it asserts, and that the resemblance is too weak, too unsampled and too unspecific to support the conclusion theology wants.
key: x resembles y in the respects cited
x arose from p by generation or vegetation
the number of members of S

lines.f: Sim(a,b), F(a) ∴ F(b), with strength proportional to Sim
lines.d: The schema of analogical inference. Philo lays the rule down himself in Part II, that wherever one departs from the similarity of the cases one diminishes proportionably the evidence, and it is that rule his three objections then work on.
lines.note: This is not a rule of any deductive system. It is a policy of proportioning belief, and it is the only rule the design argument ever uses.

lines.d: The universe resembles a machine: parts fitted to parts, means adapted to ends, throughout nature, with a nicety exceeding human contrivance.
Machines are made by intelligent designers. This is known from wide and constant experience of watches, houses, ships and looms.
By the rule at line 1: the universe too has an intelligent designer, resembling human mind in proportion as the universe resembles human contrivance.

lines.f: Card({x : x is a universe and x is observed}) = 1
lines.d: First objection. Line 3 is a sampled generalisation, and the sample of universes has exactly one member, which is the very case in question. No causal generalisation about universes has any basis.
lines.note: Philo, Part II. The point is not that the sample is small but that the reference class was never sampled at all: we have observed the origin of watches, never the origin of a world.

lines.f: Sim(w, v) ∧ Gen(p, v) ∴ ∃p Gen(p, w)
lines.d: Second objection. Substitute a different analogue into the same schema. The universe resembles an animal or a vegetable at least as well as a machine, and those arise by generation, not design.
lines.note: Philo, Part VII. The schema does not select among analogues, so it licenses generation, spinning, and the other cosmogonies Philo runs through as readily as it licenses design. Compare the schema-substitution structure of Gaunilo's island.

lines.f: ∃d D(d,w) ∧ Int(d) is no better supported than ∃d ∃d′ (d ≠ d′ ∧ D(d,w) ∧ D(d′,w))
lines.d: Third objection. Like effects prove like causes only in degree as well as kind, so the premises equally support a committee of deities, an apprentice deity, or a superannuated one.
lines.note: Philo, Part V. Nothing in lines 2 and 3 fixes uniqueness, infinity, incorporeality or moral perfection, since none of these is a feature of the human contrivance that grounds the analogy.

lines.f: Sim(cause of order in w, human intelligence) to some remote and undefined degree
lines.d: Philo's concession in Part XII. The analogy survives only as a vague proposition admitting of no application and no consequence for conduct or worship.

args.verdict: There is no fallacy to name, because there is no valid form claimed. The argument is an inductive analogy, and lines 5, 6 and 7 attack it at the three places an analogy can be attacked: the warrant for the rule, the choice of analogue, and the specificity of the conclusion. Line 7 is the most damaging, since it grants everything and still yields no God worth the name.
args.contested: Whether Philo speaks for Hume is a two-century dispute, turning on Part XII's apparent retraction; Kemp Smith (1935) held Philo is Hume throughout and the retraction ironic, while Gaskin and others read the concession as sincere. Line 5 is contested by Bayesians from Swinburne (1979) onward, who recast design as an inference to the best explanation rather than an analogy, so that the sample-of-one objection has no purchase. Line 6 lost some force after 1859, since Darwin supplied a mechanism for organised complexity rather than an alternative analogy. Line 7 is answered chiefly by an appeal to simplicity, Swinburne (1979) holding that a single infinite designer is the simpler hypothesis, a reply many find unpersuasive, which is why fine-tuning arguments tend to concede the point and argue for a designer of unspecified attributes.
args.why: The point of formalising here is to show that there is nothing to formalise, and that this is the whole objection. Displaying the schema at line 1 makes visible that the design argument's rule is a policy proportioning conclusion to resemblance, not an inference rule, and that every one of Philo's three attacks is aimed at a different component of that schema rather than at a premise. Substituting a second analogue at line 6 shows that the same schema yields incompatible cosmogonies, and line 7 shows the conclusion is not a single proposition but an unrestricted disjunction.
args.anachronism: Hume has no notion of a reference class, no probability calculus in this sense, and no way to say that a conclusion is underdetermined by evidence; lines 5 and 7 restate in modern epistemic terms objections he puts as questions in the mouth of a character.

args.sub: that the divine attributes and the existence of evil cannot all be true together
args.work: reported in Lactantius, De Ira Dei 13, c. 313-315
args.sysn: first-order logic, set out as a demonstration that a set of sentences is jointly unsatisfiable
args.claim: That the propositions asserting an omnipotent, omniscient and wholly good God and the proposition that some evil exists form an inconsistent set, so that at least one of them must be given up.
key: the God of classical theism, taken as a single being
e is an evil: a state of affairs it would be better were absent
x is able to prevent e
an arbitrary evil, taken from line 2 by existential instantiation

lines.d: The theist's claim: there is such a being, and it has all three attributes without qualification.
lines.note: Nothing in the argument requires that these be the only divine attributes, only that they be genuine ones.

lines.d: There is at least one evil. The logical version needs only one; it does not depend on how much evil there is, or of what kind.
lines.note: This is the whole of the empirical input. Everything else in the set is conceptual.

lines.d: Bridging premise on power: an omnipotent being is able to prevent any evil whatever, since a power with exceptions is not omnipotence in the sense the first line asserts.
lines.note: Attacked by anyone who holds that some goods are not available to omnipotence without their attendant evils.

lines.d: Bridging premise on knowledge: an omniscient being knows of every evil that obtains, so ignorance cannot be the explanation of why any evil is left standing.
lines.note: The least contested of the four bridges.

lines.d: Bridging premise on goodness: a wholly good being wishes to prevent every evil it knows of and is able to prevent.
lines.note: This is where the greater-good replies enter, by inserting a clause excepting evils logically required by an outweighing good.

lines.d: Bridging premise on efficacy: what an agent both wishes to prevent and is able to prevent does not obtain.
lines.note: Trivial for an omnipotent agent, and usually left tacit; it is stated here because leaving it tacit is what makes the inconsistency look immediate.

lines.d: Take any evil a. Lines 3 and 4 give knowledge and ability, line 5 then gives the wish, and line 6 then denies that a obtains at all.
The six lines cannot all be true. The argument does not conclude that God does not exist; it concludes that one of the six must be surrendered.
lines.note: Which one is surrendered is the whole subsequent history of the chain.

args.verdict: Valid. The derivation from lines 1 to 6 is impeccable, so every reply must reject a line, and lines 5 and 6 are the only ones with any real slack. The argument does not by itself refute theism; it forces a choice.
args.contested: Two things are disputed. First, the attribution: Lactantius is the only source, he gives it in his own Latin, and no surviving Epicurean text contains it. Reinhold Glei argued in 1988 that it derives from a lost Academic sceptical source, perhaps Carneades, rather than from Epicurus; others accept the attribution, and the question remains open. Second, the argument's force: J. L. Mackie, who gave the modern statement in 1955, conceded that the inconsistency emerges only with additional quasi-logical rules, and Alvin Plantinga's reply in the 1960s and 1970s turned on showing that those rules are not necessary truths. Glei's ground is not merely that the wording is Lactantius's own but that the content tells against Epicurus: the argument presupposes a god who might be expected to intervene, whereas the Epicurean gods take no interest in the world at all and so face no dilemma about permitting evil.
args.why: Set out in English the argument sounds like an immediate contradiction, and that is how it is usually quoted. The notation shows that lines 1 and 2 alone are consistent: four further quantified premises are needed before anything follows. Once they are written down it becomes visible that they are not logical truths but substantive claims about power, goodness and their relation, and that every serious reply in the next sixteen centuries is an attack on one of them, chiefly line 5.
args.anachronism: Quantified predicate logic postdates the argument by two millennia, and neither Epicurus nor Lactantius separated a logical from an evidential problem. The framing here as an inconsistent set is Mackie's, from Evil and Omnipotence (1955); the isolation of the bridging premises as the point of attack is Plantinga's.

args.n: Privation and the free will defence
args.sub: that evil is no created thing, and that a world containing free agents is worth its wrongs
args.work: De Libero Arbitrio, 388-395; Confessions VII; Enchiridion, c. 421-423
args.sysn: first-order logic extended with an alethic possibility operator, the conclusion being a consistency claim rather than a derivation of the facts
args.claim: That evil is a privation rather than a created nature, so that God is not its author, and that the proposition that God exists with all his attributes is consistent with the proposition that evil exists.
key: e is a privation: the absence of a good that ought to be present
x is a substance, a positive nature
w contains agents whose choices are free in the libertarian sense
w is better, all things considered, than w′
the conjunction asserted at line 1 of the previous entry: that God exists and is omnipotent, omniscient and wholly good
the proposition that some evil exists
the proposition that God creates agents with free will, some of whom choose wrongly

lines.d: Evil is defined as privation: not a thing but the lack of a good that should be there, as blindness is not a thing but the absence of sight.
lines.note: Taken over from Plotinus and the Neoplatonic tradition, and used by Augustine against the Manichaean doctrine of an evil principle.

lines.d: What God creates are substances, positive natures, and every such nature is good in so far as it exists.
A privation is not a substance. An absence has no positive nature of its own, and so is not the sort of item that could be brought into being at all.
God is not the author of evil. This much follows from lines 1 to 3 alone.
lines.note: It answers a charge Epicurus never made. Lines 3 to 6 of the previous entry are about preventing evils, not about creating them, and a privation can be prevented as readily as a substance.

lines.d: Some world containing free agents is better than every world containing none, even though free agents sometimes choose wrongly.
lines.note: The premise is comparative and holds of one such world, not of all of them; the stronger claim, that any free world beats any unfree one, is not needed and is not plausible.

lines.d: It is possible that God exists with all his attributes and creates free agents some of whom go wrong.
lines.note: The whole weight of the defence rests here. The claim is bare possibility, and nothing is asserted about whether it is true.

lines.d: Necessarily, if God creates free agents who choose wrongly, then some evil exists. Wrong choice is itself an evil.
Theism and the existence of evil are consistent. The conclusion is a diamond, not a bare conjunction: nothing has been shown to be true, only that nothing has been shown to be contradictory.
lines.note: Compare line 8 of the previous entry, which asserted that the same set entails absurdity. The two claims are contradictories, and the whole dispute is between them.

args.verdict: The privation half, lines 1 to 4, is valid but does not touch the inconsistent set, since that set contains no premise saying God created evil. The defence half, lines 5 to 8, is valid and does touch it: it denies line 8 of the previous entry by exhibiting a possibility. What it establishes is only possibility.
args.contested: Whether privation is a real distinction or a verbal one: pain and cruelty do not obviously reduce to absences, and the point was pressed against Augustine from the seventeenth century onward. Whether line 5 is true, since the value of libertarian freedom is exactly what a critic will deny. And whether the free will defence covers natural evil, which involves no wrong choice; Augustine appealed to the fall and to angelic wills, replies that later defenders have generally declined to reuse. Plantinga's twentieth-century version reaches line 6 by a quite different route, transworld depravity, which Augustine had no equivalent of. There is also a difficulty internal to Augustine. The freedom the early work rests on is sharply qualified by the doctrine of grace and predestination he arrives at from Ad Simplicianum (396) onward, and in the Retractationes he had to defend De libero arbitrio against Pelagian readers who quoted it back at him. Whether the mature Augustine could still run the defence at lines 5 to 8 is disputed.
args.why: The notation marks the difference between a theodicy and a defence, and the difference is a modal operator. A theodicy asserts the conjunction; a defence asserts only that it is possible. Writing line 8 with a diamond shows why the defence is both weaker and better suited to the task: it is exactly the negation of the inconsistency claim and nothing more, so it can succeed without anyone having to believe that Fw is what actually happened.
args.anachronism: Augustine drew no distinction between a defence and a theodicy; that distinction, and the practice of stating the reply as a modal consistency claim, are Alvin Plantinga's, from God and Other Minds (1967) and The Nature of Necessity (1974). Augustine took himself to be saying what is true, not what is possible.

args.n: The best of all possible worlds
args.sub: that a good, omniscient and omnipotent creator actualises the maximum of the betterness ordering
args.work: Essais de Théodicée, 1710
args.sysn: first-order logic quantifying over possible worlds, with a betterness relation among them
args.claim: That since God knows every possible world, can actualise any of them, and is wholly good, the world he actualised is the best there is, and the evils it contains are those without which it would not be the best.
key: God, omnipotent, omniscient and wholly good
w is a possible world: a maximally consistent total way things might be
w is better, all things considered, than w′
an arbitrary proposition true of the actual world

lines.d: Any two distinct possible worlds are comparable in value: one of them is better. The betterness relation connects the whole domain.
lines.note: Denied by anyone who thinks value is plural and worlds can be incommensurable.

lines.d: The ordering has a maximum: there is a world than which no possible world is better, and which is better than every other.
lines.note: A separate premise from line 1. A total ordering of an infinite domain need have no greatest element, and this is the target of the first modern objection.

lines.d: Omnipotence: every possible world lies within God's power to actualise, so the choice is made across the whole domain of worlds and not over some restricted part of it.
lines.note: Omniscience is carried in the argument by the assumption that God's choice is made over the whole domain of worlds, not over some accessible fragment.

lines.d: Goodness: a wholly good creator who knows the ordering and can reach any point in it actualises no world that some available world beats.
lines.note: This is the counterpart of line 5 of the Epicurean set, generalised from single evils to whole worlds.

lines.d: A world is actual, and it is actual because God actualised it rather than for some other reason. Creation is a choice made over the domain described in the previous lines.
The actual world is a maximum of the ordering: no possible world is better than it. The evils in it are therefore necessary to it.
First objection: suppose the worlds are ordered as the integers are, each surpassed by another and none greatest. Then line 2 is false, and with line 4 nothing at all can be created by a good God.
lines.note: Aquinas had already held that God could always have made a better world (Summa Theologiae I q.25 a.6); William Rowe revived the point in Can God Be Free? (2004), arguing that no possible being is essentially perfectly good if the series has no maximum.

lines.d: Second objection: the argument fixes the ordering by pointing at the actual world rather than the reverse. Whatever the world contains, the premises license calling it a feature of the best world.
lines.note: The conclusion therefore carries no independent grip on which world is best, and cannot be checked against anything. Voltaire's Candide (1759), written after the Lisbon earthquake of 1755, is the popular form of this complaint.

args.verdict: Valid from lines 1 to 5, and the interest lies entirely in line 2. If the betterness ordering has no maximum, the argument does not merely fail: combined with line 4 it entails that a good God creates nothing. The formalisation shows this is not a rhetorical objection but a structural one about orderings.
args.contested: Whether a maximum exists is the live question, and it is a question about the structure of the value ordering, not about God. Aquinas denied a maximum; Rowe and others argue that the denial is fatal to perfect-being theism generally, while Robert Adams has argued that a creator need only create a world good enough, not the best, so that line 4 is too strong. Separately, Leibniz's own account makes God's choice free while morally necessitated, and whether that is coherent was already disputed by Samuel Clarke in the correspondence with Leibniz of 1715-16. Adams's version of the reply is in "Must God Create the Best?" (1972), where the claim is that a creator wrongs no one by making a world that is good but surpassable, so that line 4 states a stronger demand than goodness imposes.
args.why: The English phrase best of all possible worlds hides the fact that two independent things are being assumed: that worlds can be compared at all, and that the comparison has a top. Splitting them into lines 1 and 2 shows that the objection about the largest integer is not an objection to comparison but to maximality, and that it can be granted line 1 in full. Line 8 then makes visible that the conclusion excludes no possible observation.
args.anachronism: Leibniz had a rich notion of possible worlds but no quantified logic in which to state a maximality condition, and no vocabulary of orderings without greatest elements. Presenting his argument as turning on the existence of an upper bound is a twentieth-century reconstruction, though one that Aquinas's much earlier objection shows was not invisible to the tradition.

args.sub: that the mixed phenomena of the world are not what the theistic hypothesis would lead one to expect
args.work: Dialogues concerning Natural Religion X-XI, written from the 1750s, published posthumously in 1779
args.sysn: the probability calculus: a comparison of likelihoods on two hypotheses, not a derivation
args.claim: That even granting the theistic hypothesis to be consistent with the existence of evil, the particular distribution of pain and pleasure that is actually observed is far more to be expected on the supposition of an indifferent cause than on the supposition of a good one, and so counts as evidence against the latter.
key: the hypothesis that the cause of the world is omnipotent, omniscient and wholly good
the hypothesis of indifference: the cause of the world is neither good nor malevolent
the proposition that some evil exists
the observed distribution of pain and pleasure among sentient creatures
the probability of X on the supposition of Y
that pain, and not pleasure alone, is the spur by which creatures are prompted to action
that the world is conducted by general laws rather than by particular volitions
that each creature is endowed with its powers and faculties with a great frugality
the inaccurate workmanship of the great machine of nature, whose springs run to excess or fall short

lines.d: Grant Augustine and Leibniz everything. Philo concedes at the close of Part X that consistency can be had — a mere possible compatibility, he says, is not sufficient — and that conceding it costs him nothing.
lines.note: This is the hinge of the whole entry: what follows is not an attempt to derive a contradiction from T and E.

lines.d: The observed evidence is specified as four standing circumstances of the natural order, which Philo enumerates in Part XI as the sources of nearly all the misery there is.
lines.note: They are structural features, not a tally of disasters. That is what makes the argument resistant to the reply that we cannot count evils.

lines.d: None of the four is necessary. Each could, so far as we can see, have been otherwise without any compensating loss: creatures could have been driven by diminishing pleasure rather than by pain.
lines.note: Philo does not claim to prove this, only that nothing we know of makes the contrary appear.

lines.d: The four circumstances are much less to be expected if the cause is good and able than if it is indifferent. Indifference predicts exactly this sort of mixture; benevolence does not.
lines.note: The premise that carries the argument, and the one the modern replies contest.

lines.f: Pr(T | O) / Pr(I | O) = (Pr(O | T) / Pr(O | I)) · (Pr(T) / Pr(I))
lines.d: The rule connecting likelihoods to the ratio of posterior probabilities. Whatever the prior credences were, the evidence moves the ratio by the likelihood factor.

lines.f: ∴ Pr(T | O) / Pr(I | O) < Pr(T) / Pr(I)
lines.d: The observation lowers the standing of the theistic hypothesis relative to indifference, whatever one thought before.

The conclusion is not that theism is false, and not that it is inconsistent. Philo's stated result is that the phenomena afford no inference to the moral attributes, and that indifference is the most probable hypothesis.
lines.note: Consistency, granted at line 1, is untouched at line 7. That is the point.

args.verdict: The argument is not a deduction and does not purport to be one; the inference from lines 4 and 5 to line 6 is a correct application of the probability calculus. What is disputable is line 4, the assignment of the likelihoods, and line 3, the claim that the four circumstances are dispensable.
args.contested: The standing reply is what is now called sceptical theism: that we are not epistemically positioned to assign Pr(O | T) at all, because a good and omniscient being might have reasons beyond our grasp. Stephen Wykstra put this in 1984 as a condition on reasonable epistemic access, and William Alston pressed it further; critics answer that the same scepticism would undermine any inference from the world to a designer, including the one Cleanthes wants. There is also disagreement about whether Philo speaks for Hume, given the Dialogues' closing pages, an argument running since Norman Kemp Smith.
args.why: Writing the conclusion as an inequality between ratios rather than as an entailment shows that the whole apparatus of the previous two entries has been made irrelevant rather than defeated. A defence establishes ◇(T ∧ E); a likelihood argument is untouched by that, since a hypothesis can be perfectly consistent with evidence that nonetheless disconfirms it heavily. The notation locates the change of subject exactly at line 1, where the concession is made.
args.anachronism: Hume never wrote a probability in this form. Bayes's essay appeared in 1763 and Hume gives no sign of having used it, and Part XI argues in the language of what one would antecedently expect rather than in a calculus. The Bayesian regimentation is a twentieth-century reconstruction, developed by William Rowe (1979) and, in a form that keeps Hume's hypothesis of indifference by name, by Paul Draper (1989).

args.sub: that if statements about the future are already true or false, nothing is contingent
args.work: De Interpretatione 9, 18a28-19b4
args.sysn: tense logic with a future operator and an alethic necessity, after the manner of Prior
args.claim: That from the assumption that every statement about the future is already true or already false, together with the fixity of what is already true, it follows that every future event is necessary and deliberation is idle; and that some assumption in this reasoning must therefore be rejected.
key: a sea battle takes place tomorrow
it will be the case that A
A is true at time t

lines.d: Bivalence applied to a future contingent: already today, either it is true that there will be a battle or it is true that there will not.
lines.note: Bivalence, that every statement has one of the two truth values, is distinct from excluded middle, that the disjunction of a statement and its negation holds. The distinction cannot be drawn in Aristotle's own vocabulary.

lines.d: What is already true is thereby settled: if the truth is in place today, there is nothing left tomorrow to decide.
lines.note: The premise smuggles in a step from truth to necessity. Nothing in bivalence itself supplies it.

lines.d: The same for the other disjunct: if today it is already true that there will be no battle, then no battle is possible tomorrow.
By constructive dilemma from lines 1, 2 and 3: one or other of the two outcomes is necessary.
The fatalist conclusion: it is not both possible that the battle occurs and possible that it does not. Nothing is contingent, and no deliberation makes any difference.
lines.note: Aristotle states the consequence as an absurdity, at 18b26-19a6, and everything after it in the chapter is a search for the false step.

lines.d: First reading of Aristotle's response: bivalence fails for future contingents, though excluded middle is retained. The disjunction is necessary; neither disjunct has a truth value yet.
lines.note: This is the reading behind Łukasiewicz's three-valued logic of 1920 and the many-valued and supervaluational treatments that followed.

lines.d: Second reading: bivalence stands untouched and the fault is at line 4. What is necessary is the disjunction, not either disjunct. Necessity of the consequence is not necessity of the consequent.
lines.note: On this reading lines 2 and 3 are the false premises, and the argument's error is one of modal scope rather than of semantics.

lines.d: The textual hook for the second reading: what is, necessarily is when it is, but this does not make it necessary without qualification. The qualification when it is stands at 19a23.
lines.note: The same conditional-versus-absolute scoping is what Boethius will later use against the argument from divine knowledge.

args.verdict: The fatalist argument, lines 1 to 5, is valid. Its premises are not all true, but which one to reject is exactly what the chapter does not settle unambiguously. On the first reading Aristotle denies line 1; on the second he denies lines 2 and 3 and hence the step to line 4.
args.contested: The reading has been disputed since antiquity and still is. Cicero reports at De Fato 21 that Epicurus abandoned bivalence for future contingents while Chrysippus retained it, which shows the interpretative fork was already live in the third and first centuries BCE. Ammonius and Boethius read Aristotle as holding that future contingents are not definitely true or false; Łukasiewicz took him to be denying bivalence outright; G. E. M. Anscombe, in Aristotle and the Sea Battle (1956), belongs with the readings that restrict bivalence, though without Łukasiewicz's third truth value; C. W. A. Whitaker (1996) argues instead that the chapter is not about bivalence at all, but about the rule that a contradictory pair divides the true and the false.
args.why: Two distinctions that Greek cannot mark are marked by the symbols. The first is between □(A ∨ ¬A) and □A ∨ □¬A, which line 7 sets side by side; the second is between an assignment of truth values and a claim about necessity, which lines 1 and 2 separate. Once separated it is plain that bivalence alone yields nothing fatalistic: line 2 does all the damage, and it is a metaphysical premise wearing the costume of a semantic one.
args.anachronism: Aristotle had no modal operators, no tense operators, and no notion of a truth value assigned at a time; the indexing of truth to t₁ is a modern device that arguably prejudges the question the chapter asks. Whether the chapter is even about bivalence, rather than about the necessity of outcomes, is itself among the things scholars dispute, so the choice of regimentation here is not neutral between readings.

args.n: The lazy argument and the co-fated
args.sub: that if all is fated, action is pointless, and why the inference is a scope error
args.work: reported in Cicero, De Fato 28-30 and 41-43, 44 BCE; also Origen, Contra Celsum II.20
args.sysn: propositional modal logic, the operator read as fatedness rather than logical necessity
args.claim: That the argos logos, the argument from universal fate to the pointlessness of acting, misdescribes what fate is over: the fated item is a whole causal sequence including the action, so nothing follows about what would happen were the action omitted; and that responsibility survives fate because the proximate cause of an action is the agent's own nature.
key: an action, or an assent to an impression
the agent's own nature and character: what the shape of the cylinder is to its rolling
x has an external antecedent cause: the push given to the cylinder
y is the proximate and principal cause of x
x is up to a, so that a is answerable for it

lines.d: Either it is fated that you recover from this illness or it is fated that you do not. The fatalist takes this from the universality of fate.
If your recovery is fated, you will recover whether or not you call the doctor.
lines.note: The premise reads Ft(r) as fate over the bare outcome, holding across every variation in what else happens. Nothing in line 1 licenses that reading.

lines.d: And if your not recovering is fated, then calling the doctor will not save you, so the same indifference to your action holds on this side of the disjunction.
Either way the outcome is independent of what you do, so calling the doctor is idle. This is the lazy argument, which Cicero says is so called because it would end all activity in life.
Chrysippus' correction. What fate ranges over is not the bare outcome but a complex: some things, he says, are co-fated, confatalia. That you call the doctor is fated along with your recovery.
lines.note: Cicero, De Fato 30, gives the example of Oedipus being born to Laius: the begetting is co-fated with the birth.

lines.d: The scope error made explicit. From the fatedness of a conjunction one cannot detach a claim about what would hold in the absence of one conjunct. Line 2 assumes exactly that detachment.
lines.note: The fatalist needs Ft to distribute over a counterfactual variation, and it does not. The operator's scope, not the doctrine of fate, is where the argument breaks.

lines.d: The cylinder and the cone. A push starts either rolling, but that the one runs straight and the other in a circle is owing to its own shape, not to the push.
lines.note: Reported by Cicero at De Fato 42-43 and by Aulus Gellius, Noctes Atticae VII.2.

lines.d: Fate and answerability are compatible. An action can have an external antecedent cause and still be the agent's own, because the principal cause is the agent's nature.

args.verdict: The lazy argument is invalid, and line 2 is the culprit. It equivocates between it is fated that r and it is fated that r whatever else happens, and only the second supports the conclusion. Chrysippus' positive doctrine at lines 7 and 8 is not a proof but a proposal about what responsibility requires.
args.contested: Whether the co-fated reply works or merely relocates the problem: the fatalist can grant that calling the doctor is co-fated and ask in what sense it was ever open to you not to call, which is the objection Alexander of Aphrodisias presses in De Fato. The cylinder analogy is likewise disputed, since a cylinder's shape is not up to the cylinder, and Chrysippus' opponents in antiquity already asked how a character itself produced by fate can ground praise and blame. Everything here is transmitted by hostile or secondhand sources, chiefly Cicero, Plutarch, Alexander and Gellius; no work of Chrysippus survives entire.
args.why: The English argument looks like a straightforward dilemma, and the reply about co-fated events sounds like an evasion. In notation the reply is exact: line 6 is the failure of a detachment principle, and one can check that Ft(A ∧ B) has no consequence of the form ¬B → A. The notation also shows that Chrysippus need not weaken fate at all. He concedes line 1 in full and denies only line 2, which is what makes his position determinist rather than a compromise.
args.anachronism: The Stoics had a developed propositional logic but nothing corresponding to an operator whose scope can be varied over a conjunction, and their modal notions, framed in dispute with Diodorus Cronus and Philo, are defined in terms of capacity and prevention rather than in terms of an operator. Calling the position compatibilism is a modern label, and the Up(a,x) predicate compresses a Stoic doctrine of assent that has no single-predicate equivalent.

args.sub: that divine knowledge is not foreknowledge, and that the necessity it imposes is conditional
args.work: De Consolatione Philosophiae V, prose 3-6, c. 524
args.sysn: epistemic logic with an alethic necessity operator, the issue being the scope of that operator over a conditional
args.claim: That the argument from divine knowledge to the necessity of what is known commits a scope fallacy, and that in any case God's knowledge is not located at any time, since eternity is the whole and simultaneous possession of unbounded life, so that the fixity of the past does not attach to it.
key: a future contingent proposition: that you will do a certain act tomorrow
a knows at time t that p
t is earlier than the present moment
x's life and acts fall at time t
x exists eternally, which Boethius defines as the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of unbounded life

lines.d: Knowledge is factive, and necessarily so: it is not possible for God to know something that is not the case.
God knows that you will do the act. The second premise adds nothing about when he knows it, and the crude version of the argument does not need to.
The fatalist step, as the argument is usually put: since God cannot be mistaken and knows you will do it, you cannot do otherwise.
lines.note: This is the step Boethius says all the trouble comes from, at V prose 3.

lines.d: The diagnosis, with both scopings written out. The conditional is necessary; the consequent is not. From a necessary conditional and its antecedent one detaches p, not □p.
lines.note: Boethius distinguishes simple necessity from conditional necessity and uses the example of a man walking: while he walks he necessarily walks, but he need not have walked.

lines.d: Eternity is not everlasting duration but the absence of temporal location altogether. God does not live through a sequence of moments and so does not occupy any of them.
lines.note: The Latin at V prose 6 defines eternity as interminabilis vitae tota simul et perfecta possessio.

lines.d: The necessity of the past, which the fatalist needs in order to repair line 3. What was the case at a past time is no longer alterable by anyone.
lines.note: With this premise and line 1 the fatalist derivation goes through in the modal system K, and the scope diagnosis at line 4 does not stop it.

lines.d: Line 6 has no instance to work on. There is no past time at which God knew, so his knowledge is not fore-knowledge; it is one glance at the whole, as we see a present thing without making it necessary.
lines.note: This, and not line 4, is what blocks the repaired argument. That the repaired argument needs blocking at all is what sends Ockham looking for a different move.

lines.d: Divine knowledge and the contingency of what is known are compatible: God may know that you will act, and it remain open that you do not.

args.verdict: The crude argument, lines 1 to 3, is invalid and line 4 names the fallacy exactly. But the repaired argument that adds line 6 is valid in K, so line 4 does not by itself settle anything; the real work is done by lines 5 and 7, and those depend on the doctrine of timelessness rather than on any point of logic.
args.contested: Whether timelessness helps at all. Anthony Kenny argued in 1969 that the required simultaneity relation is incoherent, since if every moment is present to God then all moments are simultaneous with one another; Eleonore Stump and Norman Kretzmann answered in 1981 with a relativised eternal-temporal simultaneity, which has itself been much attacked. Linda Zagzebski has pressed the deeper point that a timeless fact can be just as fixed and beyond our power as a past one, so the move may only rename the difficulty. Whether Boethius held that God's knowledge is causally responsible for what is known is also disputed. It is also disputed whether the scope diagnosis is Boethius' solution at all. Boethius' simple and conditional necessity are necessity relative to a nature and necessity relative to a condition, not the two scopings of a modal operator, and Marenbon has argued that the load in Book V is carried by the principle that what is known is known according to the power of the knower rather than by any distinction of scope.
args.why: Line 4 sets the two scopings side by side and the fallacy is visible in a line of symbols: □(K → p) against K → □p. That much is the cleanest scope diagnosis in the history of the subject. What the notation also shows, and what the prose conceals, is that the diagnosis is not sufficient: adding line 6 gives a valid argument to which line 4 is no answer, so the eternity doctrine at lines 5 and 7 is load-bearing rather than decorative.
args.anachronism: Boethius had no operators and no distinction between the necessity of a conditional and the necessity of a consequent stated in those terms, though he came very close in Latin with necessitas condicionis. The epistemic predicate K(g,p) and the time-indexed Kt are modern; and reading V prose 6 as a formal restriction on which propositions the necessity of the past applies to is a reconstruction shaped by the twentieth-century literature on the problem.

args.n: The past that is not yet fixed
args.sub: that God's past belief about a future free act is not a fact wholly about the past
args.work: Tractatus de praedestinatione et de praescientia Dei respectu futurorum contingentium, c. 1321-24
args.sysn: tense logic with a time-indexed necessity, the accidental necessity that attaches to the past
args.claim: That although the past is fixed and its fixity transfers along entailment, the proposition that God believed at a past time that you will act is not wholly about that past time, and so is not among the propositions the fixity of the past applies to.
key: that you will do a certain act tomorrow
God believes at t that p
t is earlier than the present moment
q is a fact about t
q is accidentally necessary as of t: q is true and it is no longer in anyone's power that q be false
q is a hard fact about t: wholly about t, entailing nothing about how things go after t
q is a soft fact about t: true at t partly in virtue of what happens after t

lines.d: The necessity of the past. What has happened is beyond anyone's power; not even God, on the standard medieval view, can bring it about that what was, was not.
lines.note: Stated here without restriction. The whole of Ockham's reply is a restriction of this line.

lines.d: Transfer of necessity: if a fact is beyond our power and it entails something, that something is beyond our power too.
lines.note: The principle the argument needs in order to get from the fixity of God's belief to the fixity of your act. Some contemporary Ockhamists reject this line instead of line 1, in the manner of the objections to van Inwagen's transfer rule for powerlessness.

lines.d: God believed, a thousand years ago, that you will do the act; and that he did so is taken to be a fact about that long-past time.
lines.note: The third conjunct is doing silent work and is precisely what Ockham will deny.

lines.d: From lines 1 and 3: it is now beyond anyone's power that God believed what he believed.
Infallibility: necessarily, if God believed it, it is so. This is Boethius' line 1 restated for a time-indexed belief, and Boethius' scope diagnosis leaves it standing.
From lines 2, 4 and 5: your act is already beyond your power. The conclusion Boethius' scope distinction does not reach, because nothing here infers □p from a detached antecedent.
Ockham's restriction of line 1. Accidental necessity attaches only to facts wholly about the past, those whose truth owes nothing to what comes later.
That God believed at t₁ that you will act is true at t₁ only in virtue of what you do tomorrow. It is therefore soft, line 7 does not apply to it, and line 4 fails.
lines.note: The power this leaves you is not a power to change the past but a power such that, had you acted otherwise, God would always have believed otherwise.

args.verdict: The fatalist derivation at lines 1 to 6 is valid, and that is why the position is hard to escape. Ockham's reply is a restriction of premise 1, not a challenge to any inference; its cost is that the hard-soft distinction must be given a principled definition, and giving one has proved difficult.
args.contested: The dispute is over how to define a hard fact without either making God's past beliefs hard by fiat or making too much of the past soft. Nelson Pike posed the modern problem in 1965; Marilyn McCord Adams offered an Ockhamist criterion in 1967 and John Martin Fischer argued through the 1980s that the proposed criteria either fail or trivialise, since on some of them the fact that Caesar died before your birth comes out soft. A second line of dispute is whether Ockham himself thought the problem soluble at all, given his remark that the way God knows future contingents cannot be expressed by us. Adams's own criterion is generally held to have failed outright rather than narrowly: it had the consequence that no fact is a hard fact, which is why the 1980s literature, from Freddoso (1983) and Hoffman and Rosenkrantz (1984) to Wierenga (1989), consists of successive attempts to replace it.
args.why: Written out, the argument shows that Boethius' scope diagnosis is not available here: line 6 is reached by transfer of accidental necessity, not by detaching a necessary consequent, so the fallacy of the earlier entry is simply absent. The formalisation also isolates the exact conjunct under attack, Ab(q,t) at line 3, and shows that Ockham is not denying line 2 but denying that line 1's antecedent is satisfied. That distinction is invisible in the prose, where both look like saying the past is not really fixed.
args.anachronism: The terms hard fact and soft fact are twentieth-century: Nelson Pike posed the problem without them in Divine Omniscience and Voluntary Action (1965), and the pair enters the literature with Marilyn McCord Adams's reply of 1967; Ockham speaks of propositions secundum vocem about the present that are secundum rem about the future. Whether the modern Ockhamist apparatus is a faithful development of his text or a new theory wearing his name is itself argued over.

args.n: The five modes and the regress of justification
args.sub: that every attempt to justify a belief must run on without end, turn back on itself, or stop at something unsupported
args.byline: Sextus Empiricus, reporting the modes ascribed to Agrippa
args.work: Outlines of Pyrrhonism I.164-77, c. 200 CE; the ascription to Agrippa is from Diogenes Laertius IX.88
args.sysn: first-order logic with a two-place justification relation and a warrant predicate
args.claim: That no belief can be shown to be warranted, because every justification offered for one either continues without end, returns to a belief it was meant to support, or terminates in an assumption that has no support of its own.
key: an arbitrary belief whose warrant is under challenge
the belief x is warranted for the inquirer
y is offered, and accepted, as justifying x
the successive members of a justificatory chain for p
y stands to x in the ancestral of J: y supports x through some finite chain of justifications
z is a final member of the chain, with no further support offered for it
the three cases distinguished at line 3

lines.d: Nothing is warranted except by something else that is itself warranted. This is what the modes of dispute and of hypothesis establish: unresolved disagreement denies standing to a claim merely asserted, and a claim merely assumed acquires none.
lines.note: Everything depends on this line, and each of the three later escapes is a denial of some property it attributes to J. Foundationalism denies it outright for a privileged class of beliefs; coherentism and infinitism accept it and quarrel about the shape a chain may take.

lines.d: A justificatory chain for p is the series produced when each support offered is itself challenged and a further support is produced for it.

The chain either has a final member or it does not, and either repeats a member or it does not. The three cases are therefore jointly exhaustive: endless, circular, or stopping at something unsupported.
lines.note: Exhaustiveness holds only for chains, that is, only if J is taken to be linear. Holistic support, in which a set of beliefs supports its members jointly rather than in series, is not one of the three.

lines.d: On the first case the demand made at line 1 is never discharged. Every member waits on the next for its warrant, and no member ever comes into possession of any.
On the second, some member depends for its warrant on itself. By line 1 its requirement is unmet, and so is the requirement of everything downstream of it.
On the third, the final member is unwarranted, so by line 1 it has nothing to transmit, and nothing standing behind it in the chain is warranted either.
Suspension of judgement follows, offered by Sextus not as a doctrine to be believed but as what is left standing once no belief can be shown to have warrant.

args.verdict: Valid. The trilemma at line 3 really is exhaustive, but only for the relation described at lines 1 and 2: linear, irreflexive, and transmitting warrant forward from a warranted source. Each later escape is the denial of one of those properties, and can be located exactly.
args.contested: Three later positions reject a different clause. Foundationalists deny line 1 for basic beliefs, which is the next entry. Coherentists, notably BonJour in 1985, deny that support is linear at all, so line 2 never gets started and case (ii) is not vicious but the normal condition of a body of belief. Infinitists, notably Peter Klein from 1999, accept the linearity and deny line 4, holding that an endless non-repeating chain is what warrant actually requires. Whether the five modes are Agrippa's is itself uncertain: Sextus never names him, and the attribution rests on Diogenes Laertius. BonJour has since abandoned coherentism and defends a foundationalism resting on a priori insight, so the denial of linearity attributed to him is a position he held rather than one he holds.
args.why: The prose trilemma sounds like a taxonomy of ways to lose an argument. Written as conditions on J, it becomes visible that exhaustiveness is not free: it is bought with the assumptions that support runs in a line, that no belief supports itself, and that warrant is inherited rather than generated. Every subsequent move in this chain is the rejection of one of those, and the notation says which.
args.anachronism: Sextus has no relation symbol, no quantifier and no predicate of warrant; the modes are presented as a practical instrument for producing suspension, not as a formal exhaustiveness proof. The packaging as a trilemma with a claim to completeness is modern, and the name usually attached to it, the Muenchhausen trilemma, is Hans Albert's from 1968. The five are the modes of dispute, of infinite regress, of relativity, of hypothesis and of reciprocity. Only three of them — regress, hypothesis and reciprocity — enter the trilemma; dispute and relativity do other work, and Sextus nowhere presents the three as a closed list of alternatives.

args.sub: that the regress stops at what cannot be doubted, and what the stopping-point costs
args.byline: René Descartes, with the objection of Antoine Arnauld
args.work: Meditations on First Philosophy, 1641; Arnauld's objection in the Fourth Objections, and the reply, published with it in 1641
args.sysn: epistemic logic with a class of basic beliefs and a warrant-transmitting relation
args.claim: That the regress halts at beliefs which are warranted without being warranted by anything else, and that all other warranted belief inherits its warrant from these by steps each of which is itself clearly perceived.
key: x is basic: warranted, but not by any other belief
the proposition that I exist, entertained by me in the entertaining of it
p is clearly and distinctly perceived
the rule of truth, the sentence displayed at line 3
the proposition that God exists and is no deceiver
y supports x through some finite chain of justifications
p is being clearly and distinctly perceived now, while the mind attends to it
p was clearly and distinctly perceived, and the perceiving is now only remembered
the two halves into which the reply at line 7 splits R

lines.d: The foundationalist architecture: a belief is warranted just in case it is basic, or else inherits warrant from a belief that is itself warranted. Line 1 of the previous entry is denied for the basic case and kept for every other.
lines.note: All three horns are blocked at once, provided the class of basic beliefs is non-empty and its membership is not simply stipulated. Both provisos have to be earned.

lines.d: The cogito supplies a non-empty base. The attempt to doubt one's own existence is defeated in the making of it, so the proposition is warranted without a supporting belief behind it.

The rule of truth, generalised in the Third Meditation from the single case of the cogito: whatever is perceived clearly and distinctly is true. Without it the base holds one proposition and nothing is built on it.

Descartes holds that the rule needs a guarantee, since an all-powerful deceiver could arrange that the mind errs even in what it perceives most clearly. Only a creator who is no deceiver secures the rule.
But the proof of God in the Third Meditation proceeds from premises held on no ground except clear and distinct perception, so whatever warrant it has depends on the rule.
Lines 4 and 5 close a cycle in the justification relation. This is Arnauld's objection, and it is exactly case (ii) of the previous entry, met in the very system built to avoid it.
lines.note: Arnauld puts it flatly: we are sure that what we clearly and distinctly perceive is true only because God exists, and we are sure that God exists only because we perceive it clearly and distinctly.

lines.f: R₁: ∀p (C₁(p) → p), with B(R₁); R₂: ∀p (C₂(p) → p), with W(R₂) → W(g); and the proof of g invokes only C₁
lines.d: The reply splits the rule in two. A perception held in present attention compels assent while it is held and needs no guarantee. What God secures is the reliability of a conclusion after attention has moved on and only the memory of having perceived it clearly remains.

The cycle is broken if and only if every step of the proof of God can be held inside a single act of present attention. That is a claim about the reach of human attention, and it is not itself something clearly and distinctly perceived.

args.verdict: The architecture at line 1 is consistent and does block the trilemma. The circle at lines 4 to 6 is a genuine cycle in the warrant relation as Descartes states the two dependences, and the reply at line 7 removes it only by splitting one node into two, at the price of resting the whole system on an empirical claim about attention made at line 8.
args.contested: What Descartes needs God for is disputed. Harry Frankfurt in 1970 read the guarantee as concerning the reliability of reason as a whole rather than the truth of particular perceptions, which changes what line 4 asserts. James Van Cleve in 1979 defended a different escape, on which each particular clear and distinct perception is certain without the general rule, so that the rule can be built from them without circularity. Willis Doney and Anthony Kenny had earlier pressed versions of it; Alan Gewirth in 1941 separated psychological from metaphysical certainty to the same end. Against all of these, critics observe that the reply saves the letter of the system by conceding that clear perception unaided cannot deliver a general result, since generality requires memory.
args.why: Written as a relation, the objection stops being a rhetorical charge of arguing in a circle and becomes a cycle in a directed graph, with named nodes. The reply then has a precise shape: it does not break an edge, it splits a node, and the notation makes the price visible, because the two new nodes have to be kept apart by a fact about how much a mind can attend to at once.
args.anachronism: Descartes has no relation symbol and does not state a criterion of warrant in general form; foundationalism as a labelled position is twentieth-century, and the biconditional at line 1 is a reconstruction from the Meditations' architectural metaphors. The C₁/C₂ distinction is Descartes' own, drawn in the Second Replies and again in the reply to Arnauld in the Fourth Replies; what is disputed is not whether it is in the texts but whether it answers the objection.

args.sub: that no inference from what has been observed to what has not can be justified without assuming what it needs to prove
args.work: A Treatise of Human Nature I.iii.6, 1739; An Enquiry concerning Human Understanding IV, published in 1748 as Philosophical Essays concerning Human Understanding and retitled in 1758
args.sysn: first-order logic, with Hume's division of warrant into the demonstrative and the experiential
args.claim: That the inference from observed cases to unobserved ones is valid only with a premise asserting the uniformity of nature, and that this premise can be neither demonstrated nor established from experience without presupposing itself.
key: x is of the observed kind, for instance bread of this appearance
x has the quality found to accompany that kind, for instance being nourishing
the uniformity principle, the conditional displayed at line 2
p is demonstrative: its denial implies a contradiction
p is established by an argument from experience
y justifies x through some finite chain of justifications

lines.d: The inference actually drawn: every A so far observed has been B, therefore every A is B, including the ones not yet observed and the ones that will be met tomorrow.
lines.note: As displayed the step is invalid, and the notation shows why in one glance: the premise is consistent with the negation of the conclusion, because the conclusion quantifies over exactly the cases about which the premise says nothing.

lines.d: The premise that would repair it: that instances of which we have had no experience resemble those of which we have. With UN added, line 1 is modus ponens and beyond dispute.

Hume's fork, applied to the warrant for UN. Whatever we can be assured of is either a relation of ideas, and demonstrable, or a matter of fact, and established from experience. There is no third source.
The first horn. That the course of nature should change is distinctly conceivable and implies no contradiction, so no demonstration of UN is to be had.
lines.note: The passage from conceivability to consistency is a premise in its own right, and one that later writers have disputed rather than granted.

lines.f: E(UN) requires J(∀x ((O(x) ∧ A(x)) → B(x)), UN)
lines.d: The second horn. An argument from experience must begin from what experience delivers, and what it delivers is a record of observed cases and nothing besides.

lines.f: that step is itself licensed only by UN; ∴ Anc(UN, UN)
lines.d: Getting from the record to UN is itself a passage from the observed to the unobserved, and so needs precisely the principle it was supposed to supply. The circle here is case (ii) of the trilemma, reached from the empiricist side.

lines.f: ¬D(UN) ∧ ¬E(UN); by line 3, UN is unsupported; ∴ the inference at line 1 is invalid without UN and unsupported with it
lines.d: Hume's own conclusion is not that inferring should stop. It is that the transition is produced by custom rather than performed by reason, so that the mind's most useful operation has no argument behind it.

args.verdict: Valid, with each horn resting on a premise that has been attacked. Line 4 turns on conceivability entailing consistency; line 6 is the sharp point of the argument and its circularity charge is exact, being a cycle of the same shape as the second Agrippan mode.
args.contested: The most persistent reply distinguishes two circularities. Line 6 charges premise-circularity, but an inductive defence of induction may be only rule-circular, using the rule without asserting it as a premise, and Max Black and Richard Braithwaite in the 1950s argued that rule-circularity is not vicious; David Papineau and James Van Cleve have developed the point. P. F. Strawson in 1952 dissolved the question, holding that asking whether induction is reasonable is like asking whether the law is legal. Hans Reichenbach in 1938 offered a pragmatic vindication: if any method succeeds, induction will. Nelson Goodman in 1955 reframed the whole problem as the new riddle, since infinitely many uniformity principles fit the same record. Whether Hume argues for scepticism at all, rather than for the narrower claim that reason is not the source of the transition, divides commentators: Don Garrett in 1997, followed by David Owen in 1999, reads the argument as a thesis in cognitive psychology with no normative conclusion, while Peter Millican reads it as sceptical and normative and argues against them.
args.why: Writing UN out shows that it is a conditional, not a report about nature, and that the two horns attack different things: line 4 attacks its modal status and line 6 attacks the route to it. The notation also separates two senses of circular that ordinary discussion runs together, and it shows the second horn's circle to have exactly the structure Sextus had already described.
args.anachronism: Hume has no quantifiers and no formal notion of validity, and never writes down a premise called the uniformity principle. The reconstruction that inserts a suppressed premise comes from Mill and from Russell, and it is contested: Garrett and Millican read Hume as arguing that no argument whatever is available, not that a particular argument has a gap in it.

args.sub: that a universal theory is refutable by one case and verifiable by none, and that this is a fact about quantifiers
args.work: Logik der Forschung, 1934; The Logic of Scientific Discovery, 1959 The English volume is not a bare translation: Popper added a long series of new appendices, and much of the apparatus of degrees of corroboration used at line 6 is worked out there rather than in the 1934 text.
args.sysn: first-order logic; modus tollens together with the asymmetry between universal and existential statements
args.claim: That no finite body of evidence entails a universal law, that a single counter-instance refutes one deductively, and that this asymmetry, rather than any account of confirmation, is what makes empirical science possible.
key: a universal hypothesis, the sentence displayed at line 1
x satisfies the antecedent condition of the law
x has the property the law predicts
a basic statement: a singular, publicly testable observation report
the total evidence so far, a finite conjunction of basic statements
the degree of corroboration of H by e

lines.d: A law is a universally quantified conditional, and its negation is purely existential. The entire asymmetry that follows is contained in this one equivalence.

No finite conjunction of favourable instances entails the law, since the conjunction is consistent with the negation of H: it says nothing whatever about the unexamined cases. Asserting H on the strength of its confirmed predictions is affirming the consequent.

One counter-instance settles the matter. This is modus tollens, valid in the weakest deductive system there is, and it is the whole of Popper's answer to Hume: science does not need an inductive inference, only this one.
lines.note: Popper writes the conditional with the initial conditions folded into the left-hand side. The next entry consists of unfolding them. Popper himself does not accept a lone anomalous report as a refutation: a falsification requires a reproducible effect, described by a low-level falsifying hypothesis that has itself been corroborated. The single counter-instance at line 3 is the logical skeleton of his view rather than his methodological rule, and Lakatos named the position that stops at the skeleton dogmatic falsificationism.

lines.d: The criterion of demarcation: a theory is empirical only if some basic statement contradicts it, that is, only if it forbids something. A theory compatible with every observation that could be made tells us nothing about the world.

The modus tollens is only as sound as its minor premise. Popper concedes that basic statements are not read off experience but accepted by decision, and that every one of them contains universal terms, so no observation statement is theory-free.
lines.note: His own image is that the piles of the empirical basis are driven into a swamp and stopped when they are firm enough for present purposes.

lines.f: c(H, e) is not a probability; ¬( (H ∧ e ∧ ¬refuted) ⊨ H )
lines.d: The positive half of the method has no deductive form at all. That H has been tested severely and not refuted entails nothing about its truth, and Popper insists corroboration is not a probability, so it entails nothing about the next prediction either.

lines.f: ∴ the asymmetry at lines 1 to 3 holds; the methodology at lines 4 to 6 is not deductive
lines.d: The logic of refutation is impeccable and narrow. What it does not obviously supply is a reason to act on a theory that has so far survived; Popper held that preferring the best-corroborated theory is rational, and his critics reply that such a preference is inductive in all but name.

args.verdict: Line 3 is valid and line 2's non-entailment is correct, so the asymmetry is real and is exactly as strong as the notation makes it. The demarcation criterion and the methodology built on it do not follow: line 5 concedes that the refuting premise is conventional, and line 6 concedes that the surviving theory is not thereby supported.
args.contested: The main objection is the subject of the next entry: the antecedent of line 3 is never H alone. Beyond that, Wesley Salmon pressed line 6 hard, arguing that without an account of why a corroborated theory is a better bet Popper cannot explain the practical use of science. Thomas Kuhn observed that theories are not in fact abandoned on a single anomaly, and Imre Lakatos rebuilt the criterion around research programmes with a protective belt, so that falsification applies to a series of theories rather than to one. Purely existential statements, such as the claim that some element has a given property, are unfalsifiable but plainly scientific, and probabilistic statements are not strictly falsifiable either; Popper handles both by methodological convention, which is a retreat from the sharpness of line 4.
args.why: The notation shows that the celebrated asymmetry is nothing but the equivalence at line 1: the negation of a universal is existential, and existential statements can be established by one case where universals cannot. It also fixes the exact boundary of what is deductive here, so that lines 5 and 6, which are ordinarily treated as footnotes, appear as the two places where the deductive backbone simply stops.
args.anachronism: Less than most entries in this chain: Popper argued in this notation himself, and the modus tollens is his. The regimentation of the demarcation criterion as an existential claim about basic statements is a later tidying of his own formulation in terms of potential falsifiers.

args.sub: that a hypothesis never meets experience alone, so a refutation lands on a conjunction and names no culprit
args.byline: Pierre Duhem and W. V. O. Quine
args.work: Duhem, La théorie physique: son objet et sa structure, 1906; Quine, Two Dogmas of Empiricism, 1951, section 6
args.sysn: propositional logic: modus tollens with a conjunctive antecedent, and De Morgan
args.claim: That an observation contrary to prediction refutes only the conjunction of the hypothesis with its auxiliaries, so that which member to abandon is not settled by the experiment and must be decided on other grounds.
key: the auxiliaries: instrument theory, initial conditions, background laws, the mathematics used
the observation statement the theory predicts
the smallest body of statements that confronts experience, according to x

lines.d: A hypothesis entails no observation statement by itself. The prediction is drawn from it together with a theory of the apparatus, a statement of the initial conditions and a quantity of background that nobody writes down.
lines.note: This line is an empirical claim about how physics is done, not a theorem. It is where Duhem's case histories and Quine's argument have to do their work, and it is the only line an opponent can reasonably attack.

lines.d: The experiment comes out against the prediction.
Modus tollens, exactly as in the previous entry. The inference is valid and its conclusion is the negation of a conjunction, which is a weaker thing than the negation of a conjunct.
