De Morgan. The experiment reports that something in the bundle is false, and assigns the falsehood to no disjunct in particular. The underdetermination is not a defect of the reasoning; it is precisely what the reasoning yields.
To reach the hypothesis one must add the auxiliaries as premises. But the auxiliaries were not under test; they were in use. The experiment supplies no support for them at all.

lines.f: ∴ for any H there is an assignment of truth values to A₁, …, Aₙ on which H survives ¬O
lines.d: Duhem's conclusion is that the experiment condemns a group and that only the physicist's judgement selects the member to give up. Quine's is stronger: any statement can be held true come what may, and by the same token none is immune from revision.

lines.f: unit(Duhem) = a mature physical theory; unit(Quine) = the whole of science
lines.d: The two versions differ in strength and should not be run together. Duhem excluded physiology and certain branches of chemistry from the thesis and appealed to the physicist's good sense to make the choice; Quine's field of force extends to logic and mathematics, and he offers only conservatism and simplicity, which are preferences rather than rules.

args.verdict: Lines 3 and 4 are valid, and the argument as logic is elementary and correct. The philosophical weight rests entirely on line 1, which is an empirical claim, and on the observation that line 4 is a disjunction: the modus tollens Popper relies on survives intact and yet tells us nothing about H.
args.contested: Adolf Gruenbaum argued in 1960 that the thesis is not demonstrable in general, since nobody has shown that a non-trivial revision of the auxiliaries is always available; that a hypothesis can in principle be saved does not mean a saving revision exists. Larry Laudan pressed the difference between a revision being possible and its being rational. Bayesians, in particular Jon Dorling in 1979 and Howson and Urbach after him, argue that the disjunction is not symmetric in practice: prior probabilities distribute the blame, and in worked historical cases they distribute it decisively, so the choice is underdetermined only by the deductive logic. Quine himself moderated the thesis in Five Milestones of Empiricism in 1975 to a holism of relevant chunks; whether the 1951 formulation was ever meant literally is disputed.
args.why: In one step the notation replaces a slogan about theories facing the tribunal of experience as a corporate body with a formula: the conclusion of the test is a disjunction with as many disjuncts as the experiment had assumptions. It also shows exactly what would be needed to blame H, namely the conjunction of the auxiliaries as an added premise, and thus why the natural response, that we know the instrument works, is a confession that the test presupposed part of what it was measuring.
args.anachronism: Duhem argues in prose about the practice of physics and has no propositional regimentation; the standard display above dates from the 1950s and 1960s. Treating it as a single Duhem-Quine thesis flattens a real disagreement, since Duhem confined the claim to physics and would have rejected the extension to logic and mathematics that gives Quine's version its force.

args.sub: that two true identity statements can differ in what they let one know, which no purely referential semantics can explain
args.work: Ueber Sinn und Bedeutung, Zeitschrift fuer Philosophie und philosophische Kritik, 1892
args.sysn: first-order logic with identity, extended by an operator for attitude reports
args.claim: That a name contributes to what a sentence says something besides the object it names, because otherwise a true identity between two names could not be informative and could not fail to license substitution in reports of belief.
key: the term 'the morning star', that is, Phosphorus
the term 'the evening star', that is, Hesperus
the reference of the term t
the thought expressed by the sentence S
the subject s knows that p
the sense of t: the mode in which its reference is presented

lines.d: The morning star is the evening star. Both terms pick out Venus, and the identity statement joining them is true.

lines.f: K(s, a = a) for any competent s, without inquiry; K(s, a = b) only by discovery
lines.d: The two identity statements differ in cognitive value. One is available to anyone who understands the terms and extends nobody's knowledge; the other was an astronomical finding and might have come out otherwise.

lines.f: Th(S) is fixed by the Rf of the parts of S and their arrangement
lines.d: The assumption under test: what a name contributes to what is said is exhausted by the object it stands for, and the thought expressed is built out of those contributions.
lines.note: This is compositionality together with a purely referential semantics. Frege keeps the first and gives up the second; a Millian keeps the second and pays at line 4.

lines.f: by 1 and 3, Th(a = a) = Th(a = b); by 2, Th(a = a) ≠ Th(a = b)
lines.d: The two sentences would express one and the same thought, being built the same way out of parts with the same semantic values. Then they could not differ in what they let a knower learn, and by line 2 they do.
A term carries a second semantic factor, the mode of presentation of its reference. The identity is informative because the senses differ, and true because the references do not.

Substitution of identicals, valid everywhere in extensional contexts, fails inside a report of belief. A person may believe the morning star is bright while disbelieving it of the evening star, and be guilty of no logical error.

Frege's diagnosis leaves Leibniz's Law untouched. Within a that-clause a term stands for what is ordinarily its sense, so a and b are not co-referential there and the substitution at line 6 was never licensed to begin with.
lines.note: The cost is that reference becomes systematically shifty, and reports of beliefs about beliefs require senses of senses without end. This is the objection pressed by Carnap and later by Davidson.

args.verdict: Valid as a reductio of line 3, given the compositionality relied on at line 4. What the argument establishes is that some second factor is needed, not that it is sense in Frege's descriptive understanding of it; the identification of the factor is where every later dispute lies.
args.contested: Russell replaced sense with description together with scope, which is the next entry. Kripke in Naming and Necessity, 1980, accepted the puzzle and denied that names have descriptive senses, holding them to be rigid designators, so that the identity at line 1 is necessary and yet known a posteriori: the difference between the two statements is then epistemic rather than semantic. Millians such as Nathan Salmon and Scott Soames accept line 4's first conjunct and deny line 2's significance, holding that the two sentences do express the same proposition and that the felt difference is a matter of guises or of pragmatics. Gareth Evans and John McDowell defended object-dependent senses against the descriptive reading. Kripke's own Puzzle about Belief, 1979, argues that the difficulty at line 6 survives every proposed solution.
args.why: Setting the two puzzles side by side in the same notation shows that they are one puzzle. The informativeness of the identity and the failure of substitution in belief reports both arise from a single assumption, that co-referential terms may be exchanged without affecting what is said, and any account that resolves one must resolve the other. The prose treats them as a puzzle and its sequel.
args.anachronism: Frege had a notation and it was not this one: the Begriffsschrift has no operator for belief, and the epistemic and doxastic operators used here are twentieth-century, from Hintikka. The now standard reconstruction of sense as a function from circumstances to reference, following Carnap's intensions, is a later theory and not obviously Frege's own, since his senses are graspable objective entities rather than functions. The rendering of Bedeutung as 'reference', standard since Black's translation, is itself a theoretical decision: the German word means meaning, and 'denotation' and 'meaning' are both in print. Reading Frege's Sinn and Bedeutung straight off as sense and reference imports a later semantic vocabulary. The rendering of Bedeutung as 'reference', standard since Black's translation, is itself a theoretical decision: the German word means meaning, and 'denotation' and 'meaning' are both in print. Reading Frege's Sinn and Bedeutung straight off as sense and reference imports a later semantic vocabulary.

args.sub: that a definite description is not a name but a triple quantified claim, so that its denial has two readings and only one is false
args.work: On Denoting, Mind 14, 1905
args.sysn: first-order logic with identity; definite descriptions eliminated in favour of quantifiers
args.claim: That a sentence of the form 'the F is G' asserts existence, uniqueness and predication together, so that it is simply false when nothing is F, and that its apparent commitment to a non-existent subject is an artefact of surface grammar.
key: the individual supposedly denoted by 'the present king of France'
x is at present king of France
arbitrary predicates, in the schema at line 2

lines.f: 'the present king of France is bald' has the surface form B(k)
lines.d: Read as subject and predicate, the sentence requires a subject. There is none, and the three available answers are all unwelcome: the sentence is meaningless, or there subsists a non-existent king for it to be about, or excluded middle fails for it.

lines.f: the F is G ≡ ∃x (F(x) ∧ ∀y (F(y) → y = x) ∧ G(x))
lines.d: The analysis. Three claims at once: something is F, at most one thing is F, and that thing is G. The description has vanished from the analysis and contributes no constituent of its own.
The sentence, analysed. It is false, and false for a reason that needs no non-existent king: its first conjunct fails, and a conjunction with a false conjunct is false.
First reading of the denial, the description taking wide scope over the negation: there is exactly one king of France, and he is not bald. This is false.
Second reading, the negation taking wide scope over the description: it is not the case that there is exactly one king of France and that he is bald. This is true.

lines.f: line 3 and line 5 are contradictories; line 3 and line 4 are contraries
lines.d: Excluded middle is untouched. What looked like a counterexample to it, since neither the king is bald nor the king is not bald seemed acceptable, was an ambiguity between two formulas that English writes with the same words.
lines.note: Russell's own terms for the two are a primary occurrence of the description, at line 4, and a secondary occurrence, at line 5; on his account 'the present King of France is not bald' is false when the occurrence is primary and true when it is secondary.

lines.f: ∴ no k is required at line 1
lines.d: The apparent ontology was produced by the surface grammar. The description is an incomplete symbol: it has no meaning in isolation, while every sentence in which it occurs has a meaning and a truth value.

lines.f: presupposition: line 3 is neither true nor false when ¬∃x K(x)
lines.d: Strawson's objection of 1950. A use of the sentence presupposes the existence of a king rather than asserting it, so where there is no king the question of truth does not arise. Russell replied in 1957 that this describes a conversational impropriety and not a third truth value.

args.verdict: Valid, and line 2 is a definition, so it cannot be false, only inadequate to English. The payoff is entirely at line 6: the two scopings are formally distinct sentences with different truth values, and the ontological problem at line 1 does not survive the distinction.
args.contested: Strawson denied at line 8 that the sentence is false, and the dispute over presupposition has never closed. Keith Donnellan in 1966 distinguished referential from attributive uses, observing that a speaker may use a description to talk about someone it does not in fact fit, which line 2 cannot register; Kripke replied in 1977 that this is speaker's reference rather than semantic reference and leaves the analysis intact. Whether descriptions are quantifiers, as Stephen Neale argued at length in 1990, or genuine singular terms carrying a presupposition, as Fregeans hold, remains live. Incomplete descriptions, such as 'the table', force either a hidden completion or a contextual restriction, neither of which is in Russell's text.
args.why: Two sentences that English cannot tell apart differ in the notation by the position of one symbol relative to one quantifier, and that difference decides their truth values in opposite directions. Nothing in the prose marks the difference at all, which is why the puzzle looked ontological. This is the standard example of a formalisation dissolving a metaphysical problem rather than answering it.
args.anachronism: Russell's own notation is not this one: in On Denoting he writes the analysis out in words and marks scope by calling an occurrence of the description primary or secondary, the inverted iota with its bracketed scope indicator arriving only with Principia Mathematica in 1910. The analysis is uncontroversially his; the claim that it captures the way English speakers use such sentences is the part Strawson denied, and it is a claim about natural language rather than about logic.

args.sub: that a sentence says something only if it can be tested, and what follows when the criterion is turned on itself
args.byline: Rudolf Carnap and A. J. Ayer
args.work: Carnap, Ueberwindung der Metaphysik durch logische Analyse der Sprache, 1932, and Testability and Meaning, 1936-37; Ayer, Language, Truth and Logic, 1936, second edition 1946
args.sysn: first-order logic with a meaningfulness predicate ranging over sentences
args.claim: That a sentence is cognitively meaningful only if it is analytic or can be tested by observation, so that the sentences of metaphysics are neither true nor false but say nothing at all.
key: the sentence p is cognitively meaningful: it says something true or false
p is analytic, or its negation is
p is conclusively verifiable by some finite set of observation statements
any predicate, in the schematic law at line 2
p is confirmable: some observation statement bears on its truth
auxiliary premises, in Ayer's first formulation
observation statements; those subscripted are logically independent of one another
the criterion itself, the sentence displayed at line 1 or line 2

lines.d: The strong criterion, current in the Vienna Circle around 1930: the meaning of a sentence is the method of its verification, and a sentence for which no verification could be described is not false but empty.

The first weakening. No universal law admits a conclusive finite verification, and neither do statements about the past or about other minds, so the criterion as first stated discards the sciences along with the metaphysics. Carnap moves to confirmation and testability in 1936.

Ayer's first formulation, from 1936. Isaiah Berlin observed that taking R to be a conditional joining any metaphysical sentence to any observation makes every S whatever yield an observation statement, so the criterion admits everything it was designed to exclude.
lines.note: Berlin made the objection in 'Verification', Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society for 1938–39, and Ayer's second edition of 1946 was written partly in answer to it.

lines.f: (¬O₁ ∧ O₂) ∨ (O₃ ∧ ¬S) is directly verifiable, since with O₁ it entails O₃; and with S it entails O₂
lines.d: Ayer's 1946 revision distinguished direct from indirect verifiability. Alonzo Church showed in 1949 that for any three logically independent observation statements the displayed disjunction satisfies the definition of direct verifiability, and that it renders S indirectly verifiable, or else its negation directly verifiable. This is a proof, not a quibble.

The criterion is itself a declarative sentence and falls within the range of its own quantifier. It is not true by definition, since it is offered as a substantive verdict on which sentences say something, and no observation bears on it either way.

lines.f: ∴ ¬M(VP), or else VP does not lie in the range of ∀p
lines.d: The two exits. Either the criterion condemns itself along with the metaphysics, or it is not a statement at all but a proposal for the construction of a language, made in a metalanguage its own quantifier does not reach.

lines.f: if VP is a proposal, then 'metaphysics is meaningless' is a recommendation and not a result
lines.d: Carnap took the second exit explicitly, treating the adoption of a linguistic framework as a practical question and the external questions about it as not theoretical at all. The price is the polemical use of the criterion: a proposal cannot show that anyone else's sentences fail to say anything.

args.verdict: Line 5 is a correct application of the criterion to itself, given only that the criterion is a sentence in the language its quantifier ranges over. Line 6 states the escape, and it is a real one, taken by Carnap and costing what line 7 says it costs. Lines 3 and 4 are independently decisive against the two published formulations, and Church's result at line 4 has never been answered on its own terms.
args.contested: Whether self-application is fatal is disputed, and the dispute is about what kind of thing the criterion is. Carnap never presented it as a factual claim: it is an explication, a proposal for a language, and on that reading line 5 misdescribes it, as Richard Creath and Michael Friedman have argued. Ayer conceded that it was a definition meant to accord with usage. Against this, if the criterion is only a recommendation it cannot support the eliminativist conclusions the Circle drew from it. Carl Hempel, in his 1950 and 1951 surveys of the empiricist criterion of meaning, documented the successive breakdowns and effectively abandoned the attempt to grade individual sentences, which is where the next entry begins.
args.why: Writing M as a predicate of sentences turns the self-application objection from a debating point into a substitution instance: VP is a sentence, and the quantifier at line 1 is unrestricted. The same notation displays the weakenings as substitutions in a single conjunct, so it is visible that each retreat from V to Cf and from Cf to indirect verifiability leaves the reductio at line 5 exactly where it was.
args.anachronism: Carnap and Ayer both wrote formally, but neither states the criterion as an object-language predicate applying to sentences of the same language. Treating M that way is the very move Carnap would resist, since he insisted on the distinction between an object language and the metalanguage in which criteria for it are laid down. The regimentation is therefore contested at precisely the point where it does its damage.

args.sub: that analyticity cannot be explained except by notions that require it, so the explication closes into a cycle
args.work: Two Dogmas of Empiricism, The Philosophical Review 60, 1951
args.sysn: informal: a directed graph of definitional dependence among analyticity, synonymy and necessity, with the cycle displayed
args.claim: That no account of analyticity has been given which does not appeal to synonymy, none of synonymy which does not appeal to necessity, and none of necessity which does not appeal back to analyticity, so that the distinction has never been drawn at all.
key: p is analytic: true in virtue of meaning, independently of fact
p is a logical truth: true under every reinterpretation of its non-logical vocabulary
the expressions t and t′ are synonymous
q results from p by putting synonyms for synonyms
every explication of x so far offered appeals to y
t and t′ are interchangeable salva veritate in every context of the language
the predicate 'analytic in the artificial language L', fixed by a semantical rule of L

lines.d: The first class of analytic truths gives no trouble. A logical truth stays true under every reinterpretation of its non-logical words, and it can be identified without any appeal to meaning.

The second class is the problem. That no bachelor is married is not a logical truth, and is called analytic only because 'bachelor' and 'unmarried man' are synonymous. The first arrow of the graph is now fixed.

lines.f: ¬Def(Syn, definition); Sv(t, t′) yields only coextensiveness in an extensional language
lines.d: Synonymy is not explained by definition, since the lexicographer's definition reports a synonymy already in place. Nor by interchangeability preserving truth, which in an extensional language delivers no more than sameness of extension, as with creature with a heart and creature with a kidney.

lines.f: Sv(t, t′) ↔ Syn(t, t′) only in a language containing □; and □p is explained as An(p); ∴ Def(Syn, □) and Def(□, An)
lines.d: Interchangeability gives synonymy only in a language rich enough to say 'necessarily'. But on the empiricist's own account, which is the account under examination, 'necessarily p' means that p is analytic. The remaining two arrows are fixed.

lines.f: Def(An, Syn), Def(Syn, □), Def(□, An): a directed cycle, no node reached from outside it
lines.d: The three arrows close. Every explicans offered lies inside the family being explicated, so nothing has been explained to anyone who did not already possess the notion in advance.

lines.f: An-for-L is fixed by a semantical rule; the general An(p, L) with L free is not
lines.d: Carnap's route through artificial languages does not break the cycle. A rule may stipulate which sentences of one language are to be called analytic, but appearing on a list under the heading 'analytic' explains nothing about what the heading means, and the general notion is what was wanted.

lines.f: ∴ no boundary has been drawn between An and its complement
lines.d: Quine's stated conclusion is that belief in such a boundary is an unempirical dogma, a metaphysical article of faith held by philosophers who had made a profession of rejecting exactly that.

lines.f: suppressed premise: (no non-circular explication of x) → (x marks no distinction)
lines.d: Grice and Strawson, in 1956, grant the cycle and deny the premise that turns it into line 7. Few philosophically interesting terms admit non-circular definition, and speakers apply this family of terms with an agreement that itself needs explaining.

args.verdict: The cycle at line 5 is exactly drawn, and Quine's charge is that precise: every explicans offered is a node inside it. The argument does not establish line 7, which needs the further premise made explicit at line 8, namely that a distinction with no non-circular explication is no distinction at all.
args.contested: Grice and Strawson, In Defense of a Dogma, 1956, is the standard reply and attacks line 8 rather than the cycle. Carnap held that analyticity is to be explicated for a formalised language and not defined for natural language, and in Meaning and Synonymy in Natural Languages, 1955, offered a behavioural criterion of the sort Quine had demanded. Hilary Putnam, in The Analytic and the Synthetic, 1962, granted Quine most of the ground while defending a narrow class of one-criterion terms. Paul Boghossian separated metaphysical from epistemic analyticity and conceded the first to Quine. Timothy Williamson, in The Philosophy of Philosophy, 2007, attacks from a different direction, from understanding without assent. Kripke's necessary a posteriori and contingent a priori sever the identification at line 4 of necessity with analyticity, which damages the cycle as drawn without restoring the distinction Quine attacked. Quine himself later conceded ground: in 'Two Dogmas in Retrospect', 1991, he allowed a notion of analyticity for sentences learned in the course of learning their words, while denying that it could carry the epistemological weight Carnap had placed on it.
args.why: Drawn as a graph, the argument becomes checkable. It has three arrows, each defended in a separate section of the paper, and the cycle is then a property of the graph rather than an accusation. That also locates the standard reply exactly: Grice and Strawson do not break an arrow, and do not claim to; they deny that a cycle is fatal, which is a claim about what explication has to accomplish, not about analyticity at all.
args.anachronism: Quine argues in prose and sequentially, through six sections, and never draws a graph. Whether the paper contains one argument or several loosely joined ones is disputed: Peter Hylton and Gary Ebbs read the circularity sections as subordinate to the positive holism of section 6, in which case treating the cycle as the paper's main argument is a later scholastic tidying of it.

args.sub: that wherever many things are F there is a single Form of F which they share
args.work: Republic X 596a; Parmenides 130e-132a; Phaedo 100c-d, c. 380-360 BC
args.sysn: second-order logic with an unrestricted comprehension principle and a term-forming operator for Forms
args.claim: Whenever two or more things satisfy the same predicate, there exists exactly one further entity, the Form of that predicate, participation in which is what makes them satisfy it.
key: x is F, for an arbitrary predicate F (large, beautiful, human)
the Form of F: the single item all the F things share
any particular thing that is F

lines.d: The datum the theory is built to explain: more than one thing answers to the same predicate. Two things are both large, both beautiful, both human.
The one-over-many principle: for every predicate that anything satisfies there is an item such that a thing satisfies the predicate exactly when it participates in that item.
lines.note: This is a comprehension schema, and its range is unrestricted: F is bound by a second-order quantifier with no condition on which predicates qualify. Everything that follows in this chain, down to 1902, comes out of that missing restriction.

lines.d: Uniqueness. Without it the principle yields some item or other for each predicate but no single Form, and the theory loses its point.

lines.f: form(F) = the unique y such that ∀x (F(x) ↔ P(x,y))
lines.d: Lines 2 and 3 together license a definite description, and the description is what the term form(F) abbreviates.
For any particular a, being F and participating in the Form of F stand or fall together. The Form is what all the F things have in common.
lines.note: The biconditional is symmetric, but Plato wants an asymmetry: a is F because it participates, not the reverse. First-order logic has no connective for that, and the loss is not cosmetic.

args.verdict: Valid, and almost trivially so: lines 4 and 5 follow from lines 2 and 3 by the logic of definite descriptions. All the weight rests on line 2, which is not an inference but a posit, and on the unexplained relation P.
args.contested: Plato himself puts the objections. Parmenides 130e-131e presses the participation relation: is the whole Form in each thing, or a part of it, and either way absurdity follows. Aristotle at Metaphysics 990b adds that the theory doubles the population of the world without explaining anything, since the Forms are not in the things they explain. Modern dispute concerns whether Plato held the principle for every predicate or only for some: Parmenides 130c-d has the young Socrates hesitate over Forms of hair, mud and dirt, which suggests he sensed that unrestricted comprehension was trouble.
args.why: The notation shows two things the prose keeps hidden. First, the theory needs a second-order comprehension principle over predicates, and states no restriction on which predicates get Forms; that is precisely the shape of the axiom Frege will write down in 1893 and Russell will break in 1902. Second, the connective available at line 5 is a biconditional, while the explanatory asymmetry Plato needs is not expressible in it, so the formalisation makes visible that participation is doing work the logic cannot underwrite.
args.anachronism: Plato has no quantifiers, no second-order variables and no comprehension schema. Reading the one-over-many as a schema over predicates is a twentieth-century reconstruction owed largely to Vlastos, and scholars disagree over whether the dialogues support a principle of unrestricted generality or only a series of local claims about particular Forms.

args.sub: that self-predication and non-identity together drive the Forms into an infinite regress
args.byline: Aristotle; the argument also appears in Plato
args.work: Metaphysics 990b17 (repeated at 1079a13) and the lost Peri Ideon; Plato, Parmenides 132a-b, c. 360-340 BC
args.sysn: first-order logic with a function symbol generating the successor Form
args.claim: The one-over-many principle, together with the claims that the Form of F is itself F and that nothing is F by participating in itself, entails an infinite hierarchy of distinct Forms of F, so the theory never completes the explanation it was introduced to give.
key: z is a Form of F
two distinct ordinary things that are F
the first and second Forms of F generated by the argument
the further Form generated when z is counted among the F things

lines.d: One over many, carried over from the previous entry: any plurality of F things shares a Form of F in which each of them participates.
Self-predication. The Form of Large is itself large; the Form of Beauty is itself beautiful. Without this the Form is not one of the items over which line 1 can be reapplied.
lines.note: Plato never asserts this as a general principle. It is read off remarks such as Phaedo 100c and Protagoras 330c-d, and whether those remarks assert identity of predicate or something weaker is the whole dispute.

lines.d: Non-identity. Nothing is F in virtue of participating in itself; the Form explains the F things by standing outside their number.
Start with the datum: two ordinary things, neither of them a Form, that are both large. Everything below is generated from this pair and lines 1 to 3 alone.
Lines 1 and 4 give a first Form; line 2 makes it large in its turn; line 3 puts it outside the pair it explains.
But a and the first Form are now two distinct large things, so line 1 applies to them and yields a second Form, distinct from the first by line 3.
The step from line 5 to line 6 can be taken again at every stage, so no finite collection of Forms satisfies lines 1 to 3 together. The explanation is never completed.

args.verdict: Valid. The regress follows from lines 1, 2 and 3, and the notation shows that all three are needed: drop any one and line 6 cannot be reached. So the theory of Forms has exactly three exits, and Plato is clearly committed to line 1 but not clearly committed to both of the others.
args.contested: Vlastos, in the Philosophical Review in 1954, showed that the Parmenides version is valid only if self-predication and non-identity are both supplied, and that Plato states neither as a premise; the argument therefore convicts the theory only on a reading Plato may not hold. Sellars replied in 1955 that the premises can be recovered from the dialogue, and Strang in 1963 and Cohen in 1971 extended the debate. Cherniss had already argued in 1944 that Aristotle systematically misreports the Academy. Peterson in 1973 proposed reading self-predication in the way Vlastos called Pauline predication, so that Largeness is large in the sense that whatever participates in it is large.
args.why: Written out, the regress shows that the objection is not a single charge but a fork with three tines, and it sorts the modern defences of the Forms by which line each abandons. Peterson's Pauline reading and the reading of Forms as standards rather than instances drop line 2. Treating a Form as F in virtue of itself, self-explanatory rather than participating, drops line 3. Stratifying the Forms so that line 1 applies only to predicates of lower type drops line 1 -- and that last exit is Russell's theory of types, arrived at for the same reason twenty-three centuries later.
args.anachronism: Aristotle gives the argument in two compressed sentences with no premises labelled. The reconstruction into lines 1 to 3, and the very names self-predication and non-identity, are Vlastos's, and his numbering is now so standard that it is easy to forget it dates from 1954 rather than from antiquity.

args.sub: that of two explanations equal in every other respect, the one positing fewer kinds of entity is to be preferred
args.work: Summa Logicae I.12 and the Sentences commentary, c. 1323; the phrase Ockham's razor is later still: novacula Occami in Froidmont, 1649, the English form only in the nineteenth century
args.sysn: no derivation: a comparative preference relation over rival explanations, with its ceteris paribus clause written out
args.claim: Where two explanations account for the same data and are equal in every other theoretical virtue, the one whose ontology is properly included in the other's is to be preferred. Nothing about which of them is true follows.
key: two rival explanations of the same subject matter
the body of data both explanations address
E is adequate to D: it explains every datum in D
a theoretical virtue, quantified over in second-order position
the list of theoretical virtues other than parsimony: fit, scope, precision, fruitfulness, simplicity of law
ceteris paribus: E₁ and E₂ are equal in every respect except ontology
the ontology of E: the kinds of entity E quantifies over
proper inclusion of one ontology in another
E₁ is to be preferred to E₂

lines.d: Adequacy. An explanation qualifies for comparison only if it covers the whole of the data; the razor is not a licence to prefer a thinner theory that explains less.
The ceteris paribus clause, spelled out: both explanations are adequate, and they agree on every virtue on the list other than parsimony.
lines.note: This line carries the entire principle. Γ is never given in full by anyone, and if it were, the chance that two live theories agreed on all of it would be small. The razor is a schema awaiting a list that has not been supplied.

lines.d: The comparison of ontologies. Note that it is stated as inclusion, not as a count: E₁ posits a proper subset of the kinds E₂ posits.
The razor itself. It is an axiom of theory choice, not a rule of inference: it takes two theories as arguments and returns a ranking.
The verdict. A ranking of two explanations against each other, with no term in it that refers to the world.
The rejected theory may be the true one, and the razor is consistent with that. Nature is not obliged to be economical; the razor never claims she is.

args.verdict: Not a derivation, and to present it as one would be a misrepresentation. Lines 1 to 5 are valid, but only because line 4 stipulates the conclusion; line 6 records that the principle is not truth-preserving, so no proposition about the world is ever detached from it. The honest verdict is that the razor is a policy for ranking rivals, and that everything contestable sits in line 2.
args.contested: The sentence entities are not to be multiplied beyond necessity, in those words, is not found anywhere in Ockham; W. M. Thorburn traced it in Mind in 1918 to a seventeenth-century Scotist, Johannes Poncius, writing in 1639. What Ockham does write is numquam ponenda est pluralitas sine necessitate, plurality is never to be posited without necessity, and frustra fit per plura quod potest fieri per pauciora, it is futile to do with more what can be done with fewer. He also holds that the principle is overridden by scripture, by evident reason and by experience, which makes it a defeasible working rule rather than a metaphysical thesis. Modern dispute concerns whether line 2 is ever satisfied, given underdetermination; whether the ordering should count kinds or individuals, Lewis's distinction of 1973 between qualitative and quantitative parsimony; and whether, as Sober argued in 2015, parsimony has any general justification at all rather than a different local one in each science.
args.why: Setting the razor out formally shows that it has no conclusion of the form therefore p. Its output at line 5 is a relation between two theories, and line 6 records that this relation is compatible with the preferred theory being false. It also shows where the argument's content actually lives: not in the comparison of ontologies at line 3, which is usually easy, but in the ceteris paribus clause at line 2, whose universal quantifier ranges over a set nobody has enumerated.
args.anachronism: Ockham has no notion of an explanation as a formal object, no set of theoretical virtues, and no preference relation. He is stating a maxim of theological and physical economy in a Latin idiom about positing things; the regimentation here is a twentieth-century reconstruction from philosophy of science, and it deliberately declines to give the razor the shape of an inference because that shape would flatter it.

args.n: Basic Law V and its collapse
args.sub: that every concept has an extension, and Russell's proof that this cannot be
args.byline: Gottlob Frege; the contradiction is Bertrand Russell's
args.work: Grundgesetze der Arithmetik I, 1893; Russell's letter of 16 June 1902; Grundgesetze II, Appendix, 1903
args.sysn: second-order logic with a term-forming operator taking concepts to objects
args.claim: Frege's Basic Law V states that concepts have the same extension exactly when the same things fall under them. Russell showed that this axiom, in a system with unrestricted second-order comprehension, proves a contradiction, and therefore proves everything.
key: x falls under the concept F, under the concept G
the extension, in Frege's term the value-range, of the concept F
defined here as: y is the extension of some concept under which x falls
the Russell concept: x is an extension that does not fall under itself
ext(R), the extension of the Russell concept
an arbitrary sentence of the system

lines.d: Basic Law V. Read right to left it says every concept has an extension; read left to right it says extensions are individuated by what falls under them.
lines.note: Frege had doubts about this axiom before Russell wrote. In the introduction to volume I he calls it the point at which a dispute might arise, and says he holds it to be purely logical while conceding that this could be contested.

lines.d: Membership, defined from extensions. Given line 1 this yields, for every concept F, the comprehension biconditional at line 3.

Naive comprehension: whatever condition you can write down carves out a set, and a thing belongs to that set exactly when it satisfies the condition. This is the one-over-many principle with a term-forming operator bolted on.
Russell's concept, 1902: being a thing that does not fall under itself. Second-order comprehension guarantees that this counts as a concept, so line 1 guarantees it has an extension.
From lines 3 and 4. Everything belongs to r exactly when it does not belong to itself.
Universal instantiation at line 5, taking x to be r itself. The diagonal step; nothing in the system forbids it, because nothing in the system restricts the range of F.
A biconditional between a sentence and its negation. In classical logic this is a contradiction outright, and no assumption was made that could be discharged: line 1 is an axiom.
By ex falso, the system proves every sentence in its language. The Grundgesetze does not merely contain an error; as a formal system it is trivial.

args.verdict: The derivation is valid and the axiom is inconsistent. There is no contested premise to argue over: line 1 is Frege's own axiom, lines 2 to 8 use only rules he accepts, and the conclusion is that the system proves everything. Frege's appendix to volume II, written while the book was in press, states that hardly anything more unwelcome can befall a scientific writer than to have a foundation of his edifice shaken after the work is finished, and concedes the collapse without reservation.
args.contested: What is disputed is only the salvage. Frege's own repair in the appendix, weakening Basic Law V to exempt the extension itself, was shown to be inconsistent too: by Lesniewski, whose proof Sobocinski published in 1949, and independently by Quine in 1955. Zermelo's separation axiom of 1908 and the cumulative hierarchy save set theory by restricting comprehension; Russell's theory of types saves it by stratifying the concepts, which is the same exit the Forms had at line 1 of the third man. Since Parsons in 1965 and Wright in 1983 it has been known that second-order logic plus Hume's Principle, which says that the number of Fs is the number of Gs exactly when the two concepts can be paired off one to one, suffices for arithmetic, and since Boolos in 1987 that it is consistent. That derivation, Frege's Theorem, shows the collapse was specific to Basic Law V and not to logicism as such. The contradiction was also found independently in Hilbert's Göttingen circle: Zermelo had it by about 1900, two years before Russell wrote, though it was Russell's letter that reached Frege and Russell's name that attached to the paradox.
args.why: The notation makes visible that Basic Law V is Plato's one-over-many with a term-forming operator attached: every concept gets an object of its own, with no restriction on which concepts qualify. The regress at the third man and the contradiction here have the same source, an unrestricted comprehension principle, and differ only in that Frege wrote his down as an axiom in a formal system, where the diagonal step at line 6 became available. This is the one entry in the chain where a philosophical position is refuted by a derivation rather than by an interpretation: no reading of the premises is in dispute, and no counter-argument is possible.
args.anachronism: Almost none, unusually. Frege wrote in his own two-dimensional Begriffsschrift, so the lines here are a transcription into linear notation rather than a reconstruction, and Russell's letter gives the contradiction in essentially this form. The only liberty is the definition of membership at line 2, which is a convenience: Frege works throughout with value-ranges and the relation of falling under a concept.

args.sub: that an identity between rigid designators, if true, is necessarily true
args.byline: Saul Kripke; the formal result is due to Ruth Barcan Marcus
args.work: Naming and Necessity, lectures of 1970, published 1972 and as a book in 1980; Identity and Necessity, 1971; the theorem in Barcan Marcus, 1947
args.sysn: quantified modal logic with Leibniz's law and the necessity of self-identity
args.claim: From the necessity of self-identity and the indiscernibility of identicals it follows that any true identity is necessarily true; if ordinary names and natural-kind terms are rigid designators, the identities they state are necessary although known only empirically.
key: an arbitrary condition on x, modal conditions included
rigid designators: terms picking out the same object in every possible world

lines.d: The necessity of self-identity. Nothing could have failed to be itself, and no philosopher in the debate denies this.
Leibniz's law, the indiscernibility of identicals. If x and y are the same object, whatever holds of the one holds of the other.
lines.note: The schematic letter F is where the argument can be resisted. Quine's objection is precisely that modal contexts are not among the F's for which substitution is safe.

lines.d: Line 2 with the condition taken to be: being necessarily identical with x. The substitution is licensed only if that counts as a genuine condition on an object.
Lines 1 and 3 by modus ponens and generalisation. Identity, where it holds, holds necessarily. Four lines, and the theorem is proved.
The contrapositive of line 4 for rigid designators, and the form in which the result is actually used: if the two could have been distinct, they are distinct.

The payoff against the mind-brain identity theory. If pain is C-fibre stimulation, it is necessarily so; but it appears possible for pain to occur without C-fibre stimulation, and by line 5 that appearance suffices.
lines.note: The identity theorist's reply is that the appearance of contingency is illusory, as with heat and molecular motion, where we pick out heat by a contingent mode of presentation. Kripke's answer is that pain is picked out by the very feeling of pain, so there is no contingent mode of presentation to blame the illusion on. That answer is contested, not conceded.

lines.d: That Hesperus is Phosphorus, and that water is H₂O, are necessary truths discovered by observation. Necessity and apriority come apart.

args.verdict: Lines 1 to 4 are valid, and valid in any modal logic with Leibniz's law and necessitated self-identity; S5 is not needed for them, only for the iterated modalities used elsewhere in Naming and Necessity. Two things are genuinely disputed: whether the substitution at line 3 is legitimate, and whether the terms in any particular target identity, such as line 6's, are rigid.
args.contested: Quine argued in Word and Object in 1960 that quantifying into modal contexts is unintelligible, so line 3 is not a substitution instance of anything. The Kripkean reply is that line 4 concerns objects, not descriptions of them, and that Frege's morning star case shows only that the identity was discovered a posteriori, not that it is contingent. There is also a priority dispute: Barcan Marcus proved the formal result in the Journal of Symbolic Logic in 1947, and whether the semantics that surrounds it, direct reference and rigid designation, is hers as well was argued sharply in the 1990s, with Quentin Smith pressing the priority claim in 1995 and Soames and others rejecting it.
args.why: Four lines show that the necessity of identity needs no premise about language at all: it is a theorem of quantified modal logic and was proved as such in 1947. Everything distinctively Kripkean lies in the interpretation, in the claim that ordinary proper names and natural-kind terms are the rigid designators the theorem quantifies over. Laying it out this way separates a theorem almost nobody disputes from an empirical claim about how words work that is disputed constantly, and it isolates line 7, where the assumed alignment of the necessary with the a priori, taken for granted from Leibniz to Kant to Ayer, comes apart.
args.anachronism: The regimentation here is Kripke's own, or close to it, so the risk is not misattribution but compression: the argument in Naming and Necessity is embedded in a theory of reference, of naming as baptism and transmission, that no four lines can carry.

args.sub: that no set of purely descriptive premises deductively entails a normative conclusion
args.work: A Treatise of Human Nature III.i.1, 1740
args.sysn: first-order logic with deontic operators, and a conservativity claim about two vocabularies
args.claim: If every premise of a valid argument is free of deontic vocabulary, the conclusion cannot be one in which deontic vocabulary occurs essentially. The deontic extension of a descriptive language is conservative over it.
key: it is obligatory, permitted, forbidden that p
the operator O occurs somewhere in the sentence C
the descriptive fragment: the sentences in which no deontic operator occurs
C is normative in the vocabulary sense
O occurs essentially in C relative to Γ
C with every occurrence of O uniformly replaced by another operator O′

lines.d: The descriptive fragment, defined by vocabulary alone: a sentence is descriptive when no deontic operator appears anywhere in it.
A first attempt at what makes a conclusion normative: it is not logically equivalent to any sentence of the descriptive fragment.

The situation Hume asks about: purely descriptive premises deductively yielding a normative conclusion. He writes that a reason should be given for what seems to him altogether inconceivable, namely how the new relation could be deduced from ones entirely different from it.
Hume's Law as usually stated: line 3 never obtains. The deontic vocabulary cannot be introduced by deduction alone.

Prior's counterexample of 1960. From the plainly descriptive premise that tea-drinking is common in England there follows the disjunction: tea-drinking is common in England, or all New Zealanders ought to be shot.
lines.note: The disjunction contains O and is not logically equivalent to any O-free sentence, so by line 2 it counts as normative. Line 4, with Norm read as at line 2, is therefore false as it stands.

lines.d: The repair. O occurs essentially only if the entailment fails when O is uniformly reinterpreted. In Prior's disjunction it does not: p entails the disjunction whatever O is taken to mean, so O occurs vacuously and the counterexample lapses.
lines.note: Pigden showed in 1989 that Hume's Law so repaired is an instance of a general conservativeness fact about first-order deduction: no predicate absent from the premises can occur essentially in the conclusion of a valid argument. True of ought, and equally of hexagonal.

args.verdict: Line 4 is false on the vocabulary criterion of line 2 and true on the essential-occurrence criterion of line 6. So the claim survives, but at a price: once repaired it is a theorem about deduction in general rather than a discovery about morals, and it establishes nothing about whether moral conclusions can be rationally grounded in facts by any means short of entailment.
args.contested: Two lines of objection. The first is Prior's, in the Australasian Journal of Philosophy in 1960, at line 5, together with his converse cases deriving an is from an ought; Pigden's 1989 reply in the same journal repairs the law and simultaneously deflates it. The second is exegetical. Hume's paragraph is interrogative: he reports being surprised by authors who slip from is to ought, and asks that a reason be given. He does not argue for a theorem. MacIntyre argued in 1959 that Hume held no unbridgeable-gap thesis at all and that the passage is directed at a particular rationalist target, and Hunter pressed the point in 1962; Anscombe's brute-facts argument of 1958 and Searle's promising derivation of 1964 both attack the substantive gap rather than the formal claim.
args.why: Regimenting the claim shows that it is not one claim but two, and that the famous one is the false one. Written with the vocabulary criterion at line 2 it is refuted by a single disjunction. Written with the essential-occurrence criterion at line 6 it is true, and its truth is a fact about deductive logic that has nothing to do with ethics: it holds verbatim for any predicate one likes. The notation thus shows why Hume's Law can be simultaneously a theorem and useless as a weapon against moral naturalism.
args.anachronism: Hume has no deontic operators, no notion of a vocabulary fragment and no conservativity results; deontic logic dates from von Wright in 1951. Presenting III.i.1 as the statement of a metatheorem is a twentieth-century construction, and the strongest objection to this entry's whole approach is that the construction attributes to Hume a claim he neither makes nor needs.

args.sub: that an act is permissible only if its maxim can be willed as a universal law
args.work: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals II, 1785, Ak. 4:421-424
args.sysn: deontic logic with an operator for what a rational agent can consistently will
args.claim: An act is permissible only if the agent's maxim passes two tests: the world in which everyone acts on it must be coherent, and the agent must be able to will that world without contradicting something she must will as a rational agent.
key: the maxim of a: the agent's subjective principle, act-type plus circumstance plus end
the world in which m holds as a universal law: everyone in those circumstances acts on m
the act-type specified in m is performable in the world in question
m is conceivable as a universal law
m can be willed as a universal law
p is something any rational agent must will
the lying-promise maxim and an act on it
the maxim of never helping anyone in need, and an act on it
x helps the agent when the agent is in need
m is a true description of the maxim on which a is done

lines.d: The formula of universal law, stated as Kant states it: a necessary condition on permissibility, not a sufficient one. The test can condemn an act; it cannot certify one.
Conceivability. The universalised world must be coherent and must still contain the act the maxim describes.
Willing. A maxim fails here when its universalised world rules out something the agent, as a rational agent with ends, cannot coherently stop willing.

Contradiction in conception, the false promise. If everyone borrowed on promises they did not intend to keep, no one would accept such a promise, and the act the maxim specifies would not be performable. The maxim annihilates itself when universalised; Kant reads this as a perfect duty.

Contradiction in the will, refusing to help. A world in which no one ever helps anyone is perfectly conceivable; what the agent cannot do is will it, since as a finite rational being with ends she must will the availability of help she may need. Kant reads this as an imperfect duty.

The standard objection. One and the same act admits more than one true maxim-description, and the test returns opposite verdicts on them. Break a promise whenever it suits me fails; break a promise when that is the only way to save a life on a Tuesday passes.
lines.note: The notation makes the trouble exact: line 1 applies the test to m(a), which is written as a function of the act, but line 6 shows it is not one. Until a canonical description is fixed, the test has no well-defined input.

args.verdict: Lines 1 to 5 are valid given the definitions at lines 2 and 3, and they do distinguish the two kinds of failure Kant distinguishes. The argument is not, however, a derivation of moral content from logic alone: it is a filter whose output is determined by its input, and line 6 shows that the input is not fixed by the act. So the formula as stated is not a decision procedure.
args.contested: Hegel's charge of empty formalism, in the Philosophy of Right at section 135, is that the test presupposes the institutions whose content it pretends to derive: property must already be granted a value before its abolition can count as a contradiction. Mill made the parallel charge in the first chapter of Utilitarianism, that Kant's argument really shows only that the consequences of universal adoption would be ones no one would choose. On the maxim-description problem, O'Neill argued in 1975 that the relevant maxim is the agent's actual underlying principle, so that tailored descriptions are self-deception rather than a loophole; Korsgaard in 1985 distinguished logical, teleological and practical readings of the contradiction in conception, each of which classifies different maxims as failures.
args.why: Written out, the formula shows two features the English hides. First, it is a conditional in one direction: permissibility implies passing the test, not the reverse, so the formula can never license an act, only rule one out, and the standard reading of Kant as generating positive duties from it needs an extra premise not present here. Second, the two kinds of failure are not two applications of one test but two different operators, at lines 2 and 3, one modal and one about the content of rational volition; separating them shows why the false-promise case and the refusing-help case behave so differently, and why only the first has the shape of a contradiction at all.
args.anachronism: Kant has no deontic logic and no possible-worlds semantics; von Wright's deontic system dates from 1951 and Kripke's semantics from 1959. The operator W in particular is a placeholder for a claim about rational volition that Kant develops over the whole second Critique, and no one holds that its logic has been captured. Scholars disagree even about whether the contradiction in conception is meant to be logical, practical or teleological, which means line 2 encodes a reading rather than a text.

args.n: The proof of the principle of utility
args.sub: that the sole evidence anything is desirable is that people actually desire it
args.work: Utilitarianism, chapter IV, first published in Fraser's Magazine in 1861 and as a book in 1863
args.sysn: first-order logic with two predicates for the two senses of desirable
args.claim: That people desire their own happiness is the only evidence available that happiness is desirable; and since each person's happiness is a good to that person, the general happiness is a good to the aggregate of all persons.
key: x is desirable in the capacity sense: x can be desired
x is desirable in the normative sense: x is worth desiring, x is a good
x is a good to a

lines.d: Mill's analogy. The only proof that an object is visible is that people see it, and this is conclusive because visibility just is the capacity to be seen.
The parallel construction. On this reading of desirable, from the fact that someone desires x it follows immediately that x is desirable. The inference is valid.

But the conclusion Mill needs is about Des′, worth desiring, and no line yet reached mentions it. The English suffix is the same in visible and desirable; the semantics is not, the first being a capacity and the second a commendation.
lines.note: This is Moore's naturalistic fallacy charge of 1903, localised. The argument is valid on either reading held fixed and invalid on the mixed reading, and only the mixed reading reaches the conclusion.

lines.d: The psychological premise: each person desires their own happiness. Mill takes this as a matter of observation, and it is the only empirical input to the proof.
By lines 2, 3 and 4: each person's happiness is a good to that person. Mill's own sentence says exactly this, and adds a therefore.

The aggregation step: the general happiness, therefore, a good to the aggregate of all persons. Two things go wrong at once. What is true of each part is inferred to be true of the whole, which is the fallacy of composition; and the beneficiary changes from a person to an aggregate, which is not a subject of desire at all.
The general happiness is the criterion of morality. Reaching it requires both the equivocation flagged at line 3 and the composition inference at line 6.

args.verdict: Invalid as a deduction, and the notation locates the two failures precisely: line 3, where the argument must slide between Des and Des′, and line 6, where a distributive claim is converted into a collective one about a new subject. Neither step can be repaired without adding a premise Mill does not supply.
args.contested: Mill's defenders deny that chapter IV offers a deduction at all. Chapter IV opens by recalling that questions of ultimate ends do not admit of proof in the ordinary acceptation of the term, and chapter I promises instead considerations capable of determining the intellect. On that reading, urged by Hall in Ethics in 1949 and later by Mandelbaum and by Crisp in 1997, the passage is an appeal to what we in fact treat as evidence for value, not an entailment, and line 3 asks for a rigour Mill disclaimed. There is a further reading of line 6 on which no composition is committed: a good to the aggregate may be a way of summing goods already established person by person rather than asserting a good for a new collective subject. What that reading gains in validity it loses in force, since a sum of separate goods gives no individual any reason to promote the sum. The two charges have different provenance. Moore's attack in Principia Ethica is the equivocation on desirable at line 3; the fallacy-of-composition reading of the aggregation step belongs to the later literature, and whether Mill commits it is exactly what Hall was denying in 1949.
args.why: Splitting desirable into two predicates shows that no single line of the proof contains both, and that the argument works only by letting one word carry the normative sense while the analogy with visibility licenses the capacity sense. Writing the aggregation step with explicit quantifiers shows something the English sentence conceals completely: the argument place for the beneficiary changes between line 5 and line 6, from a bound variable ranging over persons to a constant naming their totality. That change of argument place, not the change of quantifier, is where the step fails.
args.anachronism: Mill would not have recognised the distinction between Des and Des′ as a distinction of predicates; the machinery for it, and the label naturalistic fallacy, arrive with Moore forty years later. The regimentation is fair to what the sentences say and unfair to what the chapter announces itself to be doing, which is why the defence recorded above has force.

args.sub: that goodness cannot be identical with any natural property
args.work: Principia Ethica, sections 11-14, 1903
args.sysn: first-order logic with a predicate for open questions and an operator for what a competent speaker can settle by reflection
args.claim: For any natural property N, a competent speaker who grants that something is N can still coherently ask whether it is good; the question stays open; therefore goodness is not identical with N, and is a simple non-natural property.
key: a property variable ranging over properties
N is a natural property: pleasant, desired, conducive to survival
the question: this thing is N, but is it good?
the question s is open: a speaker who fully understands it can coherently leave it unsettled
a is a competent speaker of the language
the property heat and the property molecular motion

lines.d: The observation, offered as a schema rather than a single case: for every naturalistic analysis anyone has proposed, the question whether the analysans is good remains one a competent speaker can go on asking.
If goodness simply is the property N, then asking whether an N thing is good is asking whether an N thing is N, and no competent speaker could leave that open.
lines.note: This is the load-bearing premise, and it is not an ethical claim at all. It is a claim about identity in general: that true identities are transparent to anyone who understands both terms.

lines.d: Modus tollens on lines 1 and 2, for each natural property in turn.
Goodness is not identical with any natural property. Moore concludes that it is simple, unanalysable and non-natural, and that every naturalistic ethics rests on a fallacy.
Line 2 unpacked. To close a question by identity alone, the identity must be knowable by anyone who has mastered the two terms, without further investigation.

The reply. Heat is molecular motion and water is H₂O; these identities are true and, by the necessity of identity, necessarily true, yet they were open questions to competent speakers for centuries because they are knowable only a posteriori.
lines.note: The counterexample is not available before 1970. Until rigid designation and the necessary a posteriori were articulated, line 2 looked like a truism about meaning rather than a substantive and false thesis about identity.

lines.d: Line 2 is false, so the argument is unsound. What survives is narrower: openness shows that good and the naturalistic term differ in sense, which refutes analytic naturalism but leaves synthetic identity of the properties untouched.

args.verdict: Valid and unsound. The failure is line 2 exactly, and it is a failure about identity rather than about ethics; the argument therefore refutes the thesis that good means the same as some naturalistic term, and does not touch the thesis that goodness is the same property as some natural property.
args.contested: Frankena argued in Mind in 1939 that the argument begs the question, since whether the question is open is exactly what is at issue between Moore and the naturalist. The most influential modern objection is the one at line 6: Kripke's necessary a posteriori shows that identity does not entail transparency, and the Cornell realists, Boyd, Brink and Sturgeon, built a synthetic ethical naturalism on that opening through the 1980s. A residual defence of Moore holds that the moral case differs from the heat case because there is no independent scientific practice fixing the reference of good, so nothing plays the role that molecular theory played for heat; that defence changes the argument's basis from semantics to methodology. A separate objection, pressed by Michael Smith among others, is that the argument proves too much: it is an instance of the paradox of analysis, and would convict every correct conceptual analysis of being either trivial or false.
args.why: Written as two premises, the argument shows that the one everyone examines is the first and the one that fails is the second. The observation about open questions is not really in dispute. The transparency assumption at line 2, which no one before 1970 thought worth stating, is a general thesis about identity that is refuted by cases having nothing to do with ethics, and refuted by the theorem set out in the previous chain's Kripke entry. Formalisation is what makes the dependence visible: the strongest argument in twentieth-century metaethics turns on a premise about the metaphysics of identity that its author never wrote down.
args.anachronism: Moore argues in prose about what we can significantly ask, with no epistemic operator and no property quantifier; regimenting his schema with a second-order variable over natural properties makes the argument tidier and more general than the text, where it proceeds example by example against Bentham, Mill and Spencer.

args.sub: that I cannot know I have hands, because I cannot rule out being deceived
args.work: Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation I, 1641
args.sysn: epistemic logic with a closure axiom, plus one modal premise about experience
args.claim: That no ordinary belief about the external world amounts to knowledge, because knowing it would require knowing that one is not being systematically deceived, and that cannot be known.
key: I am deceived by a demon, so that no bodily thing exists
my total course of experience is exactly as it now is

lines.d: Epistemic closure: if I know something, and know that it entails a second thing, I know the second thing. This is the principle every later reply attacks or defends.
lines.note: Closure under known entailment, not the stronger closure under entailment simpliciter, which is refuted by any agent who fails to draw an inference.

lines.d: I know that having hands is incompatible with the demon hypothesis, since that hypothesis says there are no bodily things at all. The entailment is available by reflection alone.
lines.note: The premise is secured by defining d so that it explicitly denies bodies; weaker sceptical scenarios do not deliver it so cheaply.

lines.d: The demon hypothesis and its denial are each compatible with my experience being exactly as it now is. Nothing in what is given to me discriminates between the two.
lines.note: This is the work the demon story actually does: it establishes indistinguishability, and nothing more.

lines.d: From 3, together with the requirement that knowledge rests on evidence that discriminates the known case from the alternative. No such evidence is available here.
lines.note: The inference from 3 to 4 assumes an evidentialist and internalist condition on knowledge; externalists deny it, and this is one of the two places where the argument can be blocked.

lines.d: From the closure axiom at 1 and the known entailment at 2. If I knew I had hands, I would thereby know the demon hypothesis false.
From 4 and 5 by modus tollens. I do not know that I have hands, and by parity of reasoning I know nothing whatever about bodies.

args.verdict: Valid. The inference from 4 and 5 to 6 is modus tollens and nothing turns on it. The argument's whole weight rests on the closure axiom at line 1 and on the step from indistinguishability to ignorance at line 4; those are the only two places a reply can go.
args.contested: Fred Dretske ('Epistemic Operators', 1970) and Robert Nozick (Philosophical Explanations, 1981) reject line 1 outright: on a tracking account one can know one has hands while failing to know one is not deceived, because the first belief tracks the truth across nearby possibilities and the second does not. Relevant-alternatives theorists deny that line 3 makes the demon a relevant alternative at all. Contextualists, notably David Lewis ('Elusive Knowledge', 1996) and Keith DeRose, keep closure but let the standards shift, so that the sceptic and his opponent both speak truly in their own conversational settings. Hilary Putnam (1981) argues that the hypothesis is self-refuting for a speaker who has always been deceived.
args.why: Written out, the demon does almost none of the work by itself. Everything passes through the closure axiom at line 1 and the discriminating-evidence step at line 4; the story of the deceiver only makes line 3 plausible. The regimentation therefore predicts in advance where every reply must attack, and it shows that the vividness of the hypothesis is beside the point. Prose versions leave the impression that the doubt is generated by the strangeness of the scenario rather than by a general principle about knowledge.
args.anachronism: The closure formulation is a twentieth-century regimentation, sharpened by Dretske in 1970 and standard only afterwards. Descartes states no closure principle and does not argue for scepticism as a conclusion at all: Meditation I is a method, a staged withdrawal of assent from whole classes of belief, undertaken in order to reach the cogito and then to rebuild.

args.sub: that one cannot conceive of an unconceived thing, so to be is to be perceived
args.work: Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous I, 1713; cf. Principles of Human Knowledge §23, 1710
args.sysn: first-order logic with a conceiving operator, set out to expose a scope distinction
args.claim: That the supposition of a thing existing unconceived is not merely false but inconceivable, and therefore that existence consists in being perceived.
key: Hylas, the materialist who accepts the challenge

lines.d: The challenge Philonous issues: conceive of a tree existing unconceived by anyone. This is the wide-scope reading, in which the negation lies inside what is conceived.
lines.note: Read this way the formula says only that Hylas entertains a certain general proposition. Nothing in it locates Hylas among the conceivers of the tree.

lines.d: Any act of conceiving makes its object a thing conceived by someone, namely the conceiver. This is trivially true and is the only thing Berkeley's challenge genuinely establishes.
lines.note: Trivial because existentially generalising on the conceiver. It says nothing about objects nobody has conceived.

lines.d: The narrow-scope reading is a flat contradiction, by 2. There is no tree that Hylas conceives and that nobody conceives, since Hylas is somebody.
lines.note: The contradiction is between the third conjunct and the second, not between conceiving and unconceivedness. It would arise for any object and any conceiver.

lines.d: The wide-scope reading at line 1 is consistent. A conceiver may entertain the proposition that something is unconceived without thereby conceiving of that thing while not conceiving of it.
lines.note: One conceives that there are undiscovered islands without discovering one; the general form is unremarkable.

lines.d: The argument now concludes that an unconceived tree is impossible. But this needs the inconsistency of line 1, and only line 3 has been shown inconsistent.
lines.note: This is the fallacious step. It transfers a contradiction found in the narrow scoping to the wide scoping, which is the only one the materialist ever asserted.

lines.d: Hence esse is percipi: nothing exists unperceived, and the materialist's absolute existence outside all minds is not merely unproven but unthinkable.

args.verdict: Invalid, and the notation names the step: line 5. The contradiction established at line 3 belongs to the reading in which the conceiver stands inside the scope of the negation he asserts; the conclusion requires the impossibility of the reading at line 1, which is consistent. This is a scope fallacy, not a false premise.
args.contested: Russell, in The Problems of Philosophy (1912, ch. 4), diagnoses a confusion between the act of apprehending and the object apprehended, held together by the ambiguity of 'idea'. A. N. Prior, in 'Berkeley in Logical Form' (1955), gives the scope diagnosis directly. But the charge is resisted. André Gallois ('Berkeley's Master Argument', Philosophical Review, 1974) argues that Berkeley's target is the claim that one can conceive of a thing's existing unperceived, which requires more than entertaining a general proposition. Tom Stoneham (Berkeley's World, 2002) reads the passage as a challenge about what conception can supply rather than an inference, so that no scope confusion is committed.
args.why: The English phrase 'conceive of an unconceived tree' has one surface and two logical forms, differing only in where the negation falls relative to the conceiving operator. On the inner reading the conceiver appears within the scope of the very negation he asserts, which is why it is contradictory; on the outer reading he does not, and the outer reading is the one the materialist needs. Nothing in the dialogue's wording distinguishes them, and the fallacy is simply invisible until the operator is given an explicit scope.
args.anachronism: Berkeley had neither quantifiers nor scope notation, and the passage is cast as a rhetorical challenge staked on a single issue rather than as a derivation. Prior's regimentation of 1955 is itself the object of the dispute recorded above: whether the argument has the form given here is exactly what Gallois and Stoneham deny. The name is modern too: Gallois coined master argument in 1974, and Berkeley says only that he is content to put the whole upon this issue.

args.sub: that the sceptic's premise is less certain than the conclusion it denies
args.work: 'Proof of an External World', Proceedings of the British Academy, 1939; cf. 'A Defence of Common Sense', 1925
args.sysn: epistemic logic: one conditional, run in both directions
args.claim: That one may know one has hands, and infer from that knowledge that the sceptical hypothesis is false, with as good a right as the sceptic has to argue in the opposite direction.
key: I am deceived by a demon, so that no bodily thing exists
the certainty a rational person attaches to p

lines.d: The conditional both parties accept, obtained from closure and the known entailment. It is line 5 of the sceptical argument in contrapositive form, and neither side disputes it.
lines.note: Everything below shows that this conditional is neutral between the two positions: it is a bridge that can be crossed in either direction.

lines.d: The sceptic's premise: I do not know that I am not deceived, because no available evidence discriminates the deceived case from the ordinary one.
Moore's premise, offered by holding up first one hand and then the other. He takes himself to know this better than he knows any premise of any philosophical argument.
lines.note: Moore granted in 1939 that he could not prove it, while insisting that he knew it; the concession is what leaves the comparative judgement at line 7 carrying the whole case.

lines.d: The sceptic's derivation: modus ponens on the shared conditional. I do not know that I have hands.
Moore's derivation: modus tollens on the very same conditional. I do know that I am not deceived, because I know something that entails it.
Premises 2 and 3 are jointly inconsistent given 1. The two arguments are the same three propositions; nothing internal to the triad determines which pair to retain.
lines.note: Both derivations are valid, so validity is silent here. This is the whole content of the Moorean shift.

lines.d: The residual question is comparative: keep whichever premise is the more certain. Moore's claim is that no sceptical premise has ever been as certain as that here is one hand.
lines.note: This is not a formal question, and no calculus supplies the comparison. It is where the argument leaves logic.

args.verdict: Both derivations are valid, and they share every proposition. That is the point. Validity settles nothing, because the disagreement is over which of the inconsistent pair 2 and 3 to abandon, and line 7 makes the criterion explicit: comparative certainty, which is not a matter of logic at all.
args.contested: Whether the shift begs the question, or merely refuses one. James Pryor ('The Skeptic and the Dogmatist', 2000) defends Moore's entitlement to line 3 as immediate perceptual warrant; Crispin Wright replies that warrant fails to transmit across the conditional at line 1, so that line 5 is valid but epistemically idle. Wittgenstein, in the remarks written in 1949-51 and published as On Certainty (1969), takes a third route: 'I know' is misused at line 3. Propositions like 'here is one hand' are hinges on which doubt and inquiry turn, standing fast for us rather than being known or doubted, so both the sceptic and Moore have misdescribed their status.
args.why: Set out side by side, the two arguments contain the same three sentences and differ only in the direction of inference. That is the entire content of the Moorean shift, and prose conceals it, because in prose Moore appears to be ignoring the sceptic rather than reusing his conditional. The regimentation also shows what the shift cannot do: since both derivations are valid, no logical fault can be found on either side, and the residual question at line 7 is one of comparative credence.
args.anachronism: Moore did not present his proof as a modus tollens on a sceptical conditional, and his stated target in 1939 was Kant's complaint that the existence of things outside us must be accepted on faith for want of a proof, not Cartesian doubt. The closure conditional at line 1 is a later importation, which is what makes the symmetry with the demon argument displayable at all.

args.sub: that without a common power defection dominates, and war follows
args.work: Leviathan XIII-XVII, 1651; cf. De Cive I, 1642
args.sysn: a symmetric two-person game in normal form, decided by its payoff ordering
args.claim: That among rational agents with no enforcer, keeping covenants is dominated by breaking them, so that the outcome is universal war and a sovereign with power to punish is necessary for peace.
key: break the covenant, or strike first
the first agent's payoff when he plays x and the second plays y
the second agent's payoff, the game being symmetric
the penalty the sovereign attaches to D

lines.f: each agent chooses from {C, D}; outcomes are the four pairs
lines.d: The predicament reduced to its bones: two agents, each of whom may keep faith or break it, each choosing without knowing what the other will do.
Hobbes's ranking. Preying on a man who keeps faith is best; mutual peace next; general war next; and worst of all is keeping faith with a man who does not.
lines.note: This single line carries the argument. It is an empirical and psychological claim about men in the condition of mere nature, not anything demonstrable.

lines.d: From 2. Whatever the other man does, D pays better than C. So D strictly dominates, and the reasoning needs no estimate of the other's likely behaviour.

lines.f: (D,D) is the unique equilibrium, and (C,C) Pareto-dominates it
