lines.d: By symmetry the second agent reasons alike. Both defect, and both do worse than they would have done under mutual peace, which each of them prefers.
Covenants without the sword are but words. The condition of mere nature is a war of every man against every man, arrived at by rational agents and not by wicked ones.
The sovereign's function stated exactly: attach to defection a penalty large enough to reverse the top of the ordering. Then C dominates and peace is the equilibrium.
lines.note: The required k is large, must apply to every agent, and must be credible without exception; hence the extent of the power Hobbes assigns.

lines.d: The rival ordering, an assurance game: mutual peace is best of all, and defection is attractive only against a defector. Trust, not temptation, is what is missing.
lines.note: This is the reading on which men prefer peace but fear being caught keeping faith alone.

lines.f: under 7: no dominant strategy; (C,C) and (D,D) are both equilibria
lines.d: The problem is then coordination, not temptation. The sovereign need only make peace the salient and expected choice, and the power required is very much less than Leviathan's.

args.verdict: Valid from line 2, and only from line 2. Lines 3 to 5 follow by dominance and need no further assumption; the entire argument for absolute sovereignty is therefore an argument for one ordering of four outcomes. Lines 7 and 8 show that a nearby ordering, equally consistent with Hobbes's psychology, yields a far weaker conclusion.
args.contested: Whether Hobbes's state of nature is a prisoner's dilemma at all. David Gauthier (The Logic of Leviathan, 1969) reconstructs the anticipation argument along broadly dilemma lines, with defection dominant. Gregory Kavka (Hobbesian Moral and Political Theory, 1986), for whom most men are moderates who prefer peace to preying, and Jean Hampton (Hobbes and the Social Contract Tradition, 1986) both argue against that reading, Hampton holding that Hobbes's own reasoning turns on shortsightedness and on the fear of others rather than on dominance, which brings it closer to an assurance problem. Michael Taylor (The Possibility of Cooperation, 1987) presses a further point: iterated among people who expect to meet again, even a dilemma admits cooperative equilibria without any sovereign.
args.why: The notation shows that the conclusion requires one particular ranking of four outcomes and collapses under a neighbouring one. In prose, 'men are wicked' and 'men cannot trust one another' read as the same thought; as orderings they are different games with different remedies. Written out, the sovereign's necessary power becomes a function of the payoffs: under dominance he must permanently alter every agent's incentives, under assurance he need only make peace the expected choice, which a much smaller power can do.
args.anachronism: Hobbes had no game theory; the normal form dates from von Neumann and Morgenstern in 1944 and the prisoner's dilemma from Flood, Dresher and Tucker around 1950. More than the notation is at stake: which game Hobbes described is a live scholarly dispute, with Gauthier and Hampton on opposite sides, so lines 2 and 7 are two rival reconstructions rather than a formalisation and a variant.

args.sub: that parties behind the veil of ignorance choose the principle whose worst outcome is best
args.work: A Theory of Justice §§24-26, 1971
args.sysn: decision under uncertainty: the maximin rule set against expected utility
args.claim: That parties choosing principles of justice in ignorance of their own place in society would rationally adopt the maximin rule, and so would choose equal basic liberty together with the difference principle rather than any form of utilitarianism.
key: the set of candidate principles of justice
the set of social positions s₁…sₙ a party might occupy
the party's utility under principle a if he occupies position s
the worst outcome under a, that is min{u(a,s) : s ∈ S}
the probability the party assigns to occupying s

lines.f: choose a* ∈ A such that ∀a ∈ A: m(a*) ≥ m(a)
lines.d: The maximin rule. Rank each alternative by its worst possible outcome and take the alternative whose worst outcome is least bad, attending to nothing else.
The veil of ignorance. No party knows his class, talents, generation or conception of the good, and the parties are denied any basis for estimating the likelihoods.
lines.note: The veil fixes the shape of the outcome table. By itself it does not fix any rule for choosing from that table.

lines.f: condition (i): p is unknown and no estimate of it is reliable
lines.d: Rawls's first condition on the rationality of maximin: the situation must genuinely exclude probability estimates, rather than merely leaving them uncomfortable to make.

lines.f: condition (ii): the chooser sets little store by gains above m(a*)
lines.d: The second condition: whatever might be won beyond the guaranteed minimum matters little to him, so the upper reaches of the table need not be weighed.

lines.f: condition (iii): ∃a ∈ A, ∃s ∈ S: u(a,s) is unacceptable
lines.d: The third condition: the rejected alternatives carry outcomes one could not bear to live with, such as serfdom or the loss of basic liberty, if the worst befell.

lines.f: ∴ a* = the two principles of justice
lines.d: By 1 to 5, the parties choose equal basic liberty and the difference principle, whose worst position is better than the worst position permitted by average utility.

lines.f: if p(s) = 1/n for all s ∈ S, then EU(a) = (1/n) Σ u(a,s)
lines.d: Harsanyi's move. Ignorance of one's position is treated as equiprobability among positions, so the standard expected-utility rule applies to the very same table.
lines.note: The principle of insufficient reason. Whether ignorance licenses it is the crux; Rawls denies that it does.

lines.d: Maximising the sum divided by n is maximising average utility. The same veil, the same outcomes, a different decision rule, and the opposite principle of justice.

args.verdict: Lines 1 to 6 are valid, but conditionally: the three conditions at 3 to 5 are added to the description of the original position rather than derived from it. Line 3 is where the argument is decided, and lines 7 and 8 show why, since a rival rule applied to an identical information state yields average utilitarianism.
args.contested: John Harsanyi ('Can the Maximin Principle Serve as a Basis for Morality?', American Political Science Review, 1975), building on his equiprobability model of 1953 and 1955, argues that maximin is an irrational degree of risk aversion which, applied consistently, would forbid crossing a road. Kenneth Arrow made a related objection in 1973. Rawls's reply is that the original position is not a gamble at all: the choice is once and for all, binds one's descendants, and must meet the strains of commitment, publicity and stability, so the parties may not treat a whole life as a lottery ticket. In Justice as Fairness: A Restatement (2001) Rawls himself demoted maximin to a heuristic device.
args.why: The matrix and the rule are separable things, and the notation separates them. The veil of ignorance fixes what the parties do not know, and so fixes the shape of the outcome table; it does not fix how to choose from that table. Lines 1 and 7 apply two rules to identical information and reach opposed conclusions. The original position is therefore not neutral machinery that delivers justice as fairness on its own: the decision rule, defended at lines 3 to 5, is doing the work.
args.anachronism: Less than usual, since Rawls argues explicitly in decision-theoretic terms and presents maximin against a gain-and-loss table of his own. The reconstruction distorts him in a different way: he insisted that the argument from the original position is not merely a decision problem, and the conditions at lines 3 to 5 are offered as features of that special choice rather than as general axioms.

args.sub: that liberty upsets patterns, so no patterned principle survives voluntary transfer
args.work: Anarchy, State, and Utopia, ch. 7 (pp. 160-64), 1974
args.sysn: first-order logic quantifying over distributions, arranged as a reductio schema
args.claim: That no principle specifying that holdings be distributed according to some pattern can be realised without either being continually violated or being maintained by continual interference with voluntary exchange.
key: distributions of holdings, before and after the transfers
D satisfies the patterned principle Π under test
the set of transfers: a million spectators each pay a quarter to watch Chamberlain
every transfer in t is voluntary and made from holdings its transferor was entitled to
the distribution resulting from performing t upon D

lines.d: For reductio: suppose some patterned principle is the correct account of distributive justice, so that a distribution is just exactly when it fits the pattern.
lines.note: Π is a schematic letter. Nothing below depends on which pattern it is, which is why Nozick takes himself to have refuted patterning as such.

lines.d: Let D₁ be any distribution the principle itself endorses, chosen by its own advocate. By 1 it is just, and this is granted without argument.
lines.note: The concession is deliberate: Nozick lets the opponent pick the starting point so that no dispute about it can be raised later.

lines.d: The spectators each hand over a quarter, knowingly and willingly, from money that was theirs under D₁. Chamberlain ends the season a quarter of a million richer.
Whatever arises from a just situation by just steps is itself just. This is the transfer clause of the entitlement theory, and the load-bearing premise here.
lines.note: Nozick's own principle, stated earlier in ch. 7. Everything the argument establishes it establishes through this line.

lines.d: From 2, 3 and 4. Nobody was wronged: each party did what he was entitled to do with what was his, and no third party's holdings were touched.
But the pattern no longer holds. Any pattern other than one gerrymandered to this outcome is disturbed by a large transfer to a single man.
From 1 and 5 the pattern holds of D₂; from 6 it does not. The assumption fails, and it fails for every Π, since none was specified.

lines.f: ∴ Π is preserved only by forbidding some t with V(t)
lines.d: A patterned principle can be maintained only by continually preventing people from doing as they choose with what is theirs, or by continually taking back what they have transferred.

args.verdict: The reductio is valid. Its weight falls on line 4, the transfer principle, and on the concession at line 2 that D₁ is just without qualification. An opponent who grants both cannot escape line 8; the reply must come earlier, and Cohen's does.
args.contested: G. A. Cohen ('Robert Nozick and Wilt Chamberlain: How Patterns Preserve Liberty', Erkenntnis, 1977, developed in Self-Ownership, Freedom, and Equality, 1995) attacks line 2. The socialist grants that D₁ is just relative to the pattern under test, not that it is just simpliciter and therefore fit to serve as an untouchable fixed point; and consent to a transaction does not settle the justice of the background against which it takes place. The spectators agree to watch a game, not to a change in the structure of holdings, and their children face a distribution they never agreed to. A second line of reply, drawn from Rawls, is that principles of justice govern the basic structure and not each transaction within it, so a single transfer cannot falsify them.
args.why: Formalised, the argument has nothing to do with basketball. It is a schema with a free variable over patterned principles, valid for every instance, which is why Nozick can claim to have refuted patterning as such rather than one pattern. The notation also locates the reply precisely: Cohen does not dispute the derivation but denies that line 2's J(D₁) is available in the unqualified form line 4 needs, so that the two lines equivocate on what the opponent conceded.
args.anachronism: The transfer principle at line 4 is Nozick's own and he states the argument as general, so the schema is close to his intent. What the regimentation adds is determinacy: Π is treated as a well-defined predicate on distributions, whereas Nozick's 'patterned' is a family of cases held together by resemblance, and several of his opponents deny that their principles are patterns in his sense at all.
